Look at the children. That is a test worth running on any religion, including your own. Never mind the pedigree of the teaching or the seriousness of the people. Look at the children. Does this produce men and women who are free, free to admit failure, free to be glad, free to stop performing, or does it produce a household of anxious servants who cannot rest? Sinai was genuinely from God, and when it was used as a ladder it still bore children for slavery, because it was never given to be a ladder.

How can I tell whether my church is a Hagar church or a Sarah church? Not by the strictness of its morals, because the free children of God love his law. Ask instead what people are trusting. Is the gospel of Christ’s finished work preached clearly and often, so that sinners leave knowing they are forgiven? Do people confess sins honestly, or only hide them? Are newcomers with messy pasts welcomed as fully as long-standing members? Is obedience urged as the fruit of grace, or as the price of acceptance? Free churches can be serious about holiness; what they are not is anxious about standing.

In a sentence. These things are being taken figuratively: the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children who are to be slaves: this is Hagar. Now Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present city of Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament looking for the patterns that point to Christ. But start with what the text plainly says. When you read a story this week, ask first what happened and why it mattered then; then ask what promise it carries forward and how Christ fulfils it.

For worship. The God who wrote history wrote it in patterns, and every pattern points to his Son. Mount Sinai thundered and the people trembled at the foot of it, and could not draw near. But Christ went up a different hill, outside the present Jerusalem, and bore the curse that Sinai pronounced, so that the children of the slave woman could be born again as children of the free. The law shows us the mountain we cannot climb. The gospel shows us the Son who climbed it for us and brought us down the other side into the Father’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”

But the Jerusalem above is free. After the severity of the Hagar line, Paul gives the Galatians an address. They had been made to feel provincial: latecomers on the edge of the empire, whose membership depended on satisfying a committee far away in the real Jerusalem. Paul does not tell them to stop caring about that city. He tells them their mother lives somewhere else. The Jerusalem above is the heavenly Jerusalem: the city of God, the true people of God, the new covenant. And she is not an idea. The writer to the Hebrews says believers have already come to it: to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering (Hebrews 12:22). John sees her coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride (Revelation 21:2). The believer’s citizenship is not pending. It is filed (Philippians 3:20).

And she is our mother. Corresponding to Sarah. Believers are children of the free woman, born from above. This is why the early church could call the church a mother: not because she gives grace of herself, but because God brings his children to birth within her through the word and Spirit, and feeds and raises them there.

For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor!” Then Paul quotes Isaiah, and the quotation is one of the most beautiful moves in the letter. That is Isaiah 54:1, and where it sits matters enormously. It is the verse immediately after Isaiah 53: the very next thing said after the suffering servant is pierced for our transgressions and makes many to be accounted righteous. The barren woman is told to sing because of what the servant has just done. Her fruitfulness is purchased. That is the logic of the whole gospel in the order of two chapters, and Paul knew exactly what he was picking up.

In its own setting. In Isaiah the barren one is Zion in exile: a city stripped, emptied of her children, desolate like a barren woman, with nothing to show. God tells her to start singing before there is anything visible to sing about, because the children are coming, and there will be more of them than the woman who never lost anything ever had.

“For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.” Paul sees this fulfilled first in Sarah, who spent decades with an empty tent while Hagar had a son, and became the mother of a multitude; and then in the church: this small, unimpressive, mostly Gentile movement, the new Jerusalem gathered from every nation, will out-populate the establishment that despises it. It has. The barren woman’s children are now counted in every language on earth.

The God of barren women. Look at how God has always worked. Sarah barren, Rebekah barren, Rachel barren, Hannah barren, Elizabeth barren and old, and the line of promise runs straight through every one of them, so that when the child finally comes nobody can mistake where he came from. The barren has borne seven, sang Hannah (1 Samuel 2:5). He does not build his family out of human capacity. He never has. He waits until there is nothing left to explain it, and then he fills the tent.

A word for a particular reader. This verse will find her. Some woman reading Galatians 4 is literally barren, and has been told to rejoice by people who meant well, and it landed like a stone. The text is not asking her to pretend. Isaiah’s command to sing is addressed to a woman whose grief is real and whose situation has not yet changed: that is the whole point of the verse. And it is grounded not in optimism but in what God has promised to do. Scripture never asks anyone to feel that a loss is not a loss. It does say, here, that God’s way of filling a house has never depended on the ordinary mechanisms, that the desolate one ends the story with more, and that the emptiness he leaves in a life for a while is not a verdict on it.

Does this promise that God will give me children? No, not in the sense of a guarantee of a pregnancy. Isaiah 54 is a promise to God’s people as a whole, fulfilled in the gathering of the church, not a pledge to every childless couple. God does sometimes give children after long barrenness, and it is right to pray for them. But many faithful believers never have children, and they are not less blessed or less fruitful. In Christ, the childless are given spiritual sons and daughters, a name better than sons and daughters (Isaiah 56:4–5), and a family in the church that is as real as any household. Your fruitfulness in God’s kingdom does not depend on your womb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church replaces Israel entirely. Jewish believers are part of the Jerusalem above too, from Peter and Paul to the present day, and the free woman’s family has always had Israelites at its heart. Christians differ on what God still intends for the Jewish people as a nation (Romans 11:25–29), but all agree that there is one family of Abraham, made up of all who believe, Jew and Gentile, and that no one enters it except through Christ.

In a sentence. But the Jerusalem that is above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written: “Be glad, barren woman, you who never bore a child; shout for joy and cry aloud, you who were never in labour; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.”

On a Tuesday. When you feel small, provincial, behind, or excluded from the people who seem to matter in Christian circles, remember your address. You belong to the free city above. Live this week as a citizen of that city: unafraid of the committees, generous, glad. And if there is an empty place in your life that you have grieved for years, bring it to the God who fills tents, and ask him to make you fruitful in the way he chooses.

For worship. Before there was a single Gentile in the church, God told a barren city to sing. The Servant was crushed, and the empty tent filled, and is filling still, with children from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. The city above is free because its King paid for its freedom, and it is our mother because its King has made us its children. We are citizens of a city we have not yet seen, sung over by a God who never yet failed to fill a house he promised to fill.

parallels.desc: sing, O barren one, who did not bear

verseByVerse.quote: Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.

Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. Before the hard verse comes, the assurance. Paul tells them who they are, and he does it in the plainest terms: not candidates, not applicants, not probationers, but Isaac. The miracle child. The one nobody could have produced. The Gentile Galatians, born by God’s promise and Spirit, are like Isaac.

How do I know which son I am? A reader will not simply accept the compliment, and he is right not to. Both sons were Abraham’s. Both lived in the same tent. Ishmael was circumcised and Isaac was circumcised, and for fourteen years Ishmael was the only son in that tent, so nobody watching could have told you which line the promise was attached to. Paul has already given the test, twice, and it is not a matter of intensity. Ishmael was not less sincere than Isaac and probably worked harder. The difference is where each son came from. So ask what you are actually resting on when you are honest, and the answer usually surfaces fastest at the two extremes. After a good stretch, prayer flowing, temper holding, a real usefulness to somebody, does your confidence before God quietly rise? And after a bad one, does it fall? If it moves with your performance, you have been measuring the wrong thing, whatever you believe on paper; that confidence is Hagar’s, because it was produced by you.

You are being told your name. And the test is not what a man might expect. It is not, have I enough faith? That sends a man back inside himself to look for a quality he will never be able to weigh. Isaac did not qualify by being a better baby. He was born, and the birth was a gift, and the gift was announced before he existed. If you have come to the end of what you can contribute and are resting on what Christ has done, you are not being told to work up more assurance. You are being told your name.

But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit. Then verse 29, and it explains something the Galatians were living through and could not account for. The reference is to Genesis 21:9. On the day Isaac was weaned Abraham threw a feast, and Sarah saw Ishmael laughing, and the Hebrew word is a play on Isaac’s own name, Yitzchaq, he laughs. Ishmael was mocking the child, turning his name into a joke, at the party held in his honour. Jewish tradition expanded the scene into open persecution. It looks small in Genesis, and Paul calls it persecution, which tells you how he read it: the older brother, produced by human arrangement, could not bear the existence of the child who was pure gift. Born according to the Spirit: Isaac’s birth by God’s power, as every believer’s new birth is.

So also it is now. That is the pattern Paul says is repeating. The people persecuting the Galatian churches were not pagans. They were religious men with a claim to Abraham, and what they could not tolerate was a family they had not qualified for. The false teachers, relying on the flesh, were persecuting those who trust in the Spirit. Those who rely on human effort often oppose those who rely on grace.

Why grace provokes rage. It helps to understand why grace provokes rage rather than indifference. A man who has spent his life earning his standing has an enormous investment, and the doctrine of free grace does not merely disagree with him; it writes off the investment. If the Gentile farmer who believed last month is as accepted as the Pharisee who has kept the calendar for forty years, then the forty years bought nothing. Nobody hears that calmly. The elder brother in the parable is furious at exactly this, and he never once says an untrue thing about himself (Luke 15:29–30).

A comfort and a warning. Two things follow. The first is a comfort for anyone bruised by opposition that came from inside the church rather than outside it. Paul says so also it is now, as a settled expectation. Hostility from religious people is not evidence that you have gone wrong; it has a long pedigree, and it begins at a child’s birthday party in Genesis. The second is a warning, and it is the more useful one, because most of us are likelier to be Ishmael than Isaac on any given Tuesday. Watch what rises in you when someone is blessed without having earned it: the convert with the disgraceful history who is radiant, the newcomer given the opportunity you waited eleven years for, the brother whose prayers appear to be answered while yours are not. That flicker is not a small sin of the temperament. It is the flesh recognising the child of promise and resenting him for it.

What does persecution from religious people look like today? It is rarely violent in most Western churches, though in some places it is. More often it is mockery, suspicion and exclusion: being called careless about holiness because you preach free grace; being treated as second-class because you do not keep a group’s extra rules; being shut out of fellowship for questioning a leader. Do not exaggerate ordinary disagreement into persecution, and do not assume every critic is an Ishmael; sometimes your critics are right. But when you are opposed for trusting Christ alone, recognise the old pattern and take heart.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persecution justifies hatred in return. Believers bless those who persecute them (Romans 12:14). Isaac did not mock Ishmael back.

In a sentence. Now you, brothers and sisters, like Isaac, are children of promise. At that time the son born according to the flesh persecuted the son born by the power of the Spirit. It is the same now.

On a Tuesday. If you are opposed for trusting grace, do not be surprised. Isaac was too. And when you feel envy at grace shown to someone else, name it before God at once, then thank him for that person’s blessing out loud. Rejoicing with those who rejoice is the cure for Ishmael’s laughter.

For worship. The child of promise was mocked at his own feast, and centuries later the true Son of promise was mocked at his. They clothed him in purple, bowed to him in jest, spat on him and laughed. The flesh has always hated the gift. But the mockers could not stop the inheritance from passing to the heir, and they cannot stop it now. The laughter that belongs to Isaac, God has made laughter for me, said Sarah (Genesis 21:6), is the laughter of every child of grace, and it will outlast every sneer.

verseByVerse.quote: But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.

But what does the Scripture say? Paul has been arguing; now he stops and lets the text pronounce. Scripture settles it. And the sentence he chooses is the hardest in the chapter.

“Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.” It is Genesis 21:10, and in Genesis it is Sarah who says it, in a temper, and the thing is very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son (Genesis 21:11). What makes it Scripture rather than a domestic quarrel is verse 12, where God tells Abraham to do as Sarah says, for a reason that is not about Sarah’s feelings at all: through Isaac shall your offspring be named. God confirmed the word. The line of promise must not be confused with the line of human arrangement, and you cannot keep both in the same house pretending they are the same thing.

What is to be cast out? Read what Paul does with it. He is not issuing instructions about persons; he applies it to the two covenants he has been contrasting for ten verses. The thing that cannot stay is the system: law-keeping as the ground of acceptance, sitting alongside the gospel as a supplementary option. Law-religion and grace cannot share the inheritance. The Galatians were trying to keep both mothers in the house. Paul says the arrangement is impossible, and not because grace is intolerant. Because the two produce different children, and one of them has no share in the estate. So the Galatians should cast out the false teachers’ message, and refuse its teachers the authority to shape the church.

Not a mixture but a failure. This is where the letter is at its least accommodating and most necessary. There is no version of Christianity in which grace and merit are balanced. Add merit to grace and you do not get a moderate position; you get merit, because the moment my performance is part of the ground, the whole weight has shifted onto it. If it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6). A little law as the basis of standing is like a little water in petrol. It is not a mixture. It is a failure.

What it does not mean. It does not mean cruelty to people. It means refusing to mix law-righteousness with grace. Paul casts out a doctrine; he spends the surrounding verses in labour pains for the people who hold it, calls them his little children, and wishes he could soften his voice. Anyone who quotes verse 30 to justify being hard with a person has read the sentence and missed the chapter. And notice how Genesis itself handles Ishmael: God hears the boy crying in the desert, promises to make him a nation, and is with him as he grows (Genesis 21:17–20). The one cast out of the inheritance is not cast out of God’s care. Scripture is more tender than our use of it.

Does this mean my church should expel people who hold wrong views? Not on the strength of this verse alone. Paul’s target is a false gospel that adds works to Christ for justification, which he has already called accursed (1:8–9). A church must not let such teaching be taught from its pulpit, and teachers who persist in it after patient correction must not be given authority. Church discipline exists for that (Titus 3:10). But most disagreements among Christians are not about the ground of salvation, and they are to be borne with in love. And even those who are put out of fellowship are to be prayed for and pursued, with the aim of their restoration (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman. The chapter lands on an identity, not a warning, and the pronoun has changed: not you now, but we. Paul puts himself in the sentence with them. Believers are free children of promise, heirs of everything. Everything that follows in chapter 5 about standing firm and not submitting again to a yoke is built on this one line: for freedom Christ has set us free (5:1). He is not telling them to become free. He is telling them what they are.

How do I cast out the slave woman in my own heart? By refusing, every day, to let your performance become the ground of your standing with God. When you have a good day, do not let it make you feel more accepted; thank God for the grace that helped you. When you have a bad day, do not let it make you feel less accepted; confess it, and rest again on Christ. Throw out the inner ledger. Then obey, gladly, because the free son loves his Father’s house and his Father’s ways.

In a sentence. But what does Scripture say? “Get rid of the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son.” Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.

On a Tuesday. Listen this week for every voice that would bring you back into slavery: the preacher who says Christ is not quite enough, the friend who measures you by rules God never gave, and above all the voice in your own heart that keeps a ledger. Answer each with the last line of the chapter: I am not a child of the slave, but of the free woman.

For worship. And it is worth stopping to consider how it was done. The son of the free woman is the one who inherits, and the only Son who ever had that standing by right laid it down, was counted with the slaves, took the outsider’s place, and was cast out beyond the camp (Hebrews 13:12), so that the children of the slave woman could be brought into the house as heirs. Sarah’s son kept the inheritance because Ishmael was sent away. Ours was kept because the true Son was. Thanks be to God, we are free children of promise, and no voice on earth or in hell can send us back into slavery.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman with her son

You did me no wrong.<sup>13</sup>You know it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first,<sup>14</sup>and though my condition was a trial to you, you did not scorn or despise me, but received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.<sup>15</sup>What then has become of your blessedness? For I testify to you that, if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me.<sup>16</sup>Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?<sup>17</sup>They make much of you, but for no good purpose. They want to shut you out, that you may make much of them.<sup>18</sup>It is always good to be made much of for a good purpose, and not only when I am present with you,<sup>19</sup>my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!<sup>20</sup>I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, for I am perplexed about you.<sup>21</sup>Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?<sup>22</sup>For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.<sup>23</sup>But the son of the slave was born according to the flesh, while the son of the free woman was born through promise.<sup>24</sup>Now this may be interpreted allegorically: these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar.<sup>25</sup>Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia; she corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.<sup>26</sup>But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.<sup>27</sup>For it is written, “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor! For the children of the desolate one will be more than those of the one who has a husband.”<sup>28</sup>Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise.<sup>29</sup>But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.<sup>30</sup>But what does the Scripture say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.”<sup>31</sup>So, brothers, we are not children of the slave but of the free woman.

5.title: For Freedom Christ Has Set Us Free: The Spirit and the Flesh
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the hinge on which the entire letter turns from theology to life. The freedom Paul has argued for throughout — freedom from the law as a system of justification, freedom from the curse, freedom from the elementary principles of the old age — must now be shown to produce not moral chaos but something far better than law-keeping ever could. The chapter answers two questions that the letter’s argument raises: What does this freedom look like in practice? And what is its alternative to the law as the shaping force of Christian behavior?

The answer to the first question is given negatively and positively. Negatively: freedom is not license (“do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh”). The Judaizers’ accusation — that a gospel without law-requirements would produce moral anarchy — is not left unanswered. But the answer is not to reinstate the law; the answer is to walk in the Spirit. Positively: the whole law is fulfilled in one word — “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (v. 14). Those who walk by the Spirit do not need the law to produce love, because the Spirit is the Spirit of the God who is love, and his fruit in the believer is love. The Judaizers’ program produced biting and devouring; the Spirit produces love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

The heart of the chapter is the contrast between the works of the flesh (vv. 19–21) and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 22–23). The language itself is instructive: works (plural, produced by human striving) versus fruit (singular, the organic product of the Spirit’s life within). The flesh produces a catalogue of self-serving, community-destroying behaviors; the Spirit produces a coherent, integrated character that is nothing less than the character of Christ. The goal of the Christian life is not the avoidance of the flesh’s works by rule-keeping but the cultivation of the Spirit’s life by staying close to the one who gives it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 1 compresses four chapters into a line: for freedom Christ has set us free. The apparent tautology is the point — freedom is the destination, not a stage on the way to a stricter religion. Stand firm is a military verb, because freedom is not a resting state; slavery is restful in a way liberty is not, since a slave always knows where he stands. The yoke of slavery is Peter’s own phrase for the law at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:10), and it sits against the yoke Jesus offers in Matthew 11:29–30. Nobody goes without a yoke; the question is whose.

Verses 2–3 are the warning. If a man accepts circumcision as what completes his standing, Christ is of no advantage to him — not less, none, because he has changed systems into one that has no column for what somebody else has done. Verse 3 closes the escape route: he is obligated to keep the whole law, not the one item he was sold. Verse 4 states the result in two phrases that describe a change of position rather than of behaviour: severed from Christ, fallen out of the sphere of grace. Verse 5 draws the line with an emphatic we ourselves, and adds the note of waiting; v. 6 says neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts, but faith working through love.

Then the appeal. Verse 7 uses a technical word for cutting in on a runner — somebody stepped into their lane. Verse 8 says quietly that this persuasion is not from him who calls them. Verse 9 warns that a little leaven changes the whole loaf, invisibly, while it is happening. Verse 10 is the surprise: Paul is confident about them, in the Lord, and leaves the troubler to God. Verse 11 shows what was being said about him and names the offence of the cross, and v. 12 aims a deliberately shocking wish at teachers who make the knife the mechanism.
verseByVerse.theology:
Freedom as the Goal of Redemption, and What Falling from Grace Means

The Reformed tradition has always held that gospel freedom is more than freedom from sin’s penalty; it is freedom from performance-based religion — liberty to live as sons rather than as slaves calculating wages. This is not antinomianism. The law’s moral demands are fulfilled from within by those who walk in the Spirit rather than imposed from without on those who must earn a standing. Luther’s paradox holds both: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all.

Verse 4 must be read for what it says. Both its clauses describe position, not conduct: the people addressed have become more religious, not less, and Paul identifies them in the same breath as those who would be justified by the law. To fall from grace here is to step off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, where Christ’s work is inoperative — not to have disgraced oneself, which is the phrase’s modern and quite different meaning. That Paul writes v. 10 six sentences later, expressing confidence about the very same people, settles how v. 4 is functioning: it is the warning that prevents the thing it describes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Circumcision was offered to the Galatians as an upgrade — a fuller belonging. Verses 2–3 show it is not an upgrade but an exchange, and v. 3 reads them the rest of the contract nobody mentioned. Verse 11 reveals that Paul was being quoted against himself, perhaps on the strength of his past; his answer is his scars. Verse 12 would have landed with local force, since the mother goddess, whose chief shrine was at Pessinus, was served by priests who castrated themselves.

Now:Standing firm (v. 1) usually means refusing to answer “where do I stand with God today?” by reaching for the last few days. Verse 4 describes a man at peace with being justified by his own record, which is the opposite of the reader it frightens; and v. 8 gives a usable test for any new teaching — does it come to you the way the God who called you came to you?

verseByVerse.quote: For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.

Meaning first. Galatians 5 turns from argument to application: what does freedom in Christ mean in practice? First, stand firm in it. To accept circumcision as necessary for salvation would be to abandon Christ and fall from grace; believers wait for the hope of righteousness by faith through the Spirit, and what counts is faith working through love (vv. 1–12). Second, freedom is not licence. Believers are called to freedom, but not to indulge the flesh; rather to serve one another in love, which fulfils the law (vv. 13–15). Third, the way to live free is to walk by the Spirit. The flesh and the Spirit are at war within the believer. The works of the flesh are obvious, from sexual immorality to envy and drunkenness, and those who live by them will not inherit the kingdom. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh; so let them keep in step with the Spirit (vv. 16–26). The chapter is the portrait of a freed people, and every line of it is drawn from the face of their Liberator.

For freedom Christ has set us free. Everything Paul has argued for four chapters is now compressed into one line, and it is the line the letter is remembered by. The first clause looks like a stammer. Why say it twice? Because Paul is answering a question nobody had thought to ask: what is the freedom for? And his answer is that it is not a stage on the way to something else. It is not a probationary liberty granted so that you can demonstrate you deserve something better, nor a release so that you can be transferred to a stricter and more mature religion. Freedom (eleutheria) is the purpose of Christ’s work. Christ did not free us so that we could become slaves again; he released his people because he wanted them free.

Free from what, and free for what? Free from the law as a way of righteousness, from its curse (3:13), from the guardians and the elementary principles (4:1–9), from sin’s slavery, and from the endless anxious question of whether you have done enough. And free for God: to call him Father, to obey him from the heart, to love your neighbour without calculating. That needs saying, because a great many Christians treat grace as the doorway and law as the corridor beyond it. They will tell you cheerfully that they were saved by grace, and then describe a daily life in which everything depends on their performance. Paul says the door and the corridor are made of the same thing.

Stand firm therefore. The verb is stēkete, from stēkō, and it is a military word: hold your ground, do not give it up. Which tells you something about freedom that nobody expects: it is not a resting state. Freedom must be defended. Left alone, a free man drifts back toward slavery, because slavery is restful in a way that liberty is not. A slave is told what to do and knows exactly where he stands. Freedom requires you to live without a scoreboard, and a great many people find that harder than obedience.

And do not submit again to a yoke of slavery. A yoke was the wooden frame laid across the shoulders of working animals: a picture of burden and servitude. The rabbis spoke of the yoke of the law as a good thing, a glad discipline. But Peter, at the Jerusalem council, called it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). And it sits against another use of the word that every reader should hear beside it, because Jesus also offers a yoke: take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). So the question is never whether a man will wear a yoke. It is whose.

Again. The verb is passive: do not let yourselves be subjected. Nobody was going to force the Galatians. They were going to agree to it, for reasons that felt like devotion. And again is the sharpest word in the sentence, because these were Gentiles who had never been under Moses in their lives. Paul means that a return to law-keeping would land them back where their paganism had them: performing, appeasing, never sure.

What standing firm looks like. So what does standing firm actually look like on a Wednesday? Mostly it looks like refusing to answer one question the way your instincts want to answer it. The question is, where do I stand with God today? The instinctive answer reaches for the last few days: how you prayed, how you spoke to your wife, whether you did the thing you promised yourself you would stop doing. Standing firm is declining to answer it that way. Not because the week does not matter; it matters a great deal. But it is not the ground you are standing on, and the day you let it become the ground, the yoke is back on your shoulders and nobody had to put it there.

What it does not mean. It does not mean freedom to do whatever we like. Verse 13 rules that out. Christian freedom is not the absence of a master; it is the exchange of a cruel one for a kind one.

Is it legalism to keep personal rules, like not drinking or fasting on Fridays? Not in itself. A Christian may freely adopt a rule for wisdom’s sake: to avoid a temptation, to discipline the body, to serve a weaker brother (Romans 14:21; 1 Corinthians 9:27). It becomes a yoke of slavery in two ways: when you think keeping it makes you more acceptable to God, and when you bind it on other Christians as though God had commanded it. So keep your rule if it helps you, hold it loosely, never use it to measure others, and never let it whisper that you are more pleasing to God than the brother who does not keep it.

In a sentence. It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery.

On a Tuesday. Are there religious rules you have taken on as if they made you more acceptable to God? Lay them down, and stand in Christ’s freedom. Tomorrow morning, before you look at how yesterday went, say aloud where you stand: in Christ, accepted, free. Then go and live the day as a free man serving a good Master.

For worship. Christ did not buy us out of the market to put us to work in a new one. He bought us to bring us home. The Son of God took the yoke of the law on his own shoulders, carried it the whole way without stumbling, and then bore its curse on a cross, so that the beam would never be laid on ours again. The only yoke he lays on us now is his own, and it is shaped by the hands of a carpenter who is gentle and lowly in heart. Free indeed, because the Son has set us free (John 8:36).
verseByVerse.note: A yoke was the wooden frame joining working animals — a picture of burdensome obligation.

verseByVerse.quote: Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.

Look: I, Paul, say to you. He stops the argument and puts his name in the sentence. It is emphatic, with full apostolic authority. The whole weight of his apostleship, defended at length in chapters 1 and 2, is being set down on what comes next, and what comes next is the most alarming sentence in the letter.

That if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you. Not less advantage. None. And that is startling, because on the face of it circumcision is a small thing: a rite God himself commanded, which Paul elsewhere says counts for nothing either way (v. 6), and which he had personally arranged for Timothy (Acts 16:3). So the act is not the issue. The issue is what it is being asked to do. If a man accepts circumcision as the thing that completes his standing with God, he has not added a little security to Christ. He has changed systems. He is trusting in law-keeping, not Christ. And in the system he has entered, Christ is not an asset, because that system does not deal in gifts. It deals in obligations, and it has no column for what somebody else has done. Christ plus circumcision equals Christ of no value. You cannot have Christ as a partial Saviour.

But Paul circumcised Timothy. A reader who knows his New Testament raises an entirely fair objection here, and Paul’s opponents were evidently raising it too (v. 11). Paul circumcised Timothy. He refused to let Titus be circumcised (2:3). How is that not simple inconsistency? Because the two cases are opposite in everything that matters. Titus was a test case: the demand was made in Jerusalem, as a condition, to prove that a Gentile could not be fully accepted otherwise. Paul refused, and says he did not yield even for a moment, because the truth of the gospel was on the table. Timothy was a different situation entirely. His mother was Jewish, so in the eyes of every synagogue in the region he was a Jew who had been left uncircumcised, and that fact would have shut the door of every building Paul wanted to preach in. Nobody was claiming it justified him. It was a matter of access, not of standing.

The principle. So the same physical act meant two irreconcilable things, and Paul’s judgement in each case was governed by one question: is anyone claiming this is necessary? When nobody is, it is a matter of freedom and he is flexible to the point of inconvenience. The moment somebody says you must, he will not move an inch. That principle is worth carrying well beyond circumcision. There are a hundred secondary practices in church life, and the same believer may rightly take them up in one setting and refuse them in another, and be entirely consistent both times.

May Christians circumcise their sons today, for health or family reasons? Yes. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything (v. 6). Paul himself had Timothy circumcised for the sake of his witness among Jews (Acts 16:3). What is forbidden is circumcision as a requirement for being accepted by God. A Jewish Christian parent may circumcise his son as a mark of his heritage; no one may make it a condition of salvation.

What would circumcision be today? Anything added to Christ as a condition of being right with God. Nobody in your church is likely to demand circumcision, but plenty of things play its part: a particular experience you must have had, a style of worship, a political position, a level of Bible knowledge, a list of things good Christians do not do, a baptism in the right church, or a feeling of being sufficiently sorry. Any of these can be a good thing or a matter of conviction. The moment it becomes Christ and something, it becomes Christ of no advantage. Ask of any teaching: does it leave Christ standing alone as my whole righteousness?

I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law. Then verse 3, and it closes the escape route. The Judaizers were selling one item. Paul says there is no such thing as one item. Circumcision is not a one-off ritual; it signs you up to the whole law (James 2:10). The law is a single garment, and a man who takes hold of a corner of it has taken hold of all of it: every clause, every festival, every sacrifice, for life, without a single failure. Nobody was offering that in the sales pitch. Paul reads them the whole contract. If you choose the law, you must keep all of it, perfectly. No one can.

What it does not mean. It does not mean circumcision as a medical or cultural practice is sinful. Paul circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3). He speaks of circumcision as a requirement for righteousness.

In a sentence. Mark Paul’s words! He, Paul, tells you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all. Again he declares to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obligated to obey the whole law.

On a Tuesday. Finish this sentence honestly: I am right with God because Christ died and rose for me, and because I... If anything comes after the and, cross it out. Then live today out of the first half alone, and do your good works as a thank you, not as a down payment.

For worship. Christ is all-sufficient, and he will not share his throne with a ritual. He did not come to make up the difference between our best efforts and God’s standard; he came to be the whole of our righteousness, because our best efforts were part of the problem. He kept the whole law, every clause of it, for those who never could, and paid its whole penalty for those who broke it. Nothing can be added to a finished work. We rest in it, and the resting is our praise.

verseByVerse.quote: You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.

You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace. This is the verse in Galatians that frightens people, and it should be handled with care, because the reader most likely to be holding it is not a Judaizer. He is a Christian who has had a bad year, or a bad decade, and who has just read fallen away from grace and gone cold. So begin with what the sentence actually says, because the popular use of the phrase has almost nothing to do with it.

Not a scandal. In ordinary speech, to have fallen from grace means to have disgraced yourself: a scandal, a moral collapse, a public fall. Paul is not describing that at all. The people he is addressing have not fallen into sin. They have become more religious, not less. They are keeping a calendar and considering a rite, and they are doing it in order to please God more thoroughly. To fall from grace is not to fall into sin, as people often think, but to fall into law-righteousness: leaving the sphere of grace for the sphere of works.

Two changes of position. Look at the two halves of the sentence and the meaning is plain. Both describe a change of position, not a change of behaviour. Severed renders katargeō: to be rendered inoperative, cut off, separated, disconnected from any benefit. And Paul says who it applies to in the same breath: you who would be justified by the law. Seeking justification by the law means cutting yourself off from Christ; you cannot hold on to both. And fallen away is ekpiptō, falling out of grace as out of a place: you have stepped off the ground of grace onto the ground of law, and grace is where Christ does his work.

The lifeboat. Think of a man in a lifeboat who decides to swim alongside it, still holding the rope. He has not stopped believing in the boat. He has simply stopped being in it, and the boat is doing nothing for him while he is out there. That is Paul’s point. He is not telling the Galatians that God has thrown them out. He is telling them what law-standing does: it does not add to Christ’s work, it replaces it, and there is no arrangement in which a man is partly justified by each.

Hold it beside verse 10. Six sentences later, written to the same people in the same breath, Paul says: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. The man who has just written verse 4 is confident about them. Which tells you exactly what verse 4 is for. It is not a verdict passed on the Galatians; it is the warning that will keep them from the thing described, and the warning works by being heard.

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall from grace? Some take this verse to mean true believers can lose their salvation: Arminian Christians read it that way, holding that the Galatians were real believers who could forfeit their salvation by trusting in the law, and they are right that the warning is real and must not be blunted. Verdict: Paul is describing the meaning and consequence of seeking justification by law: it is a rejection of grace and Christ. Those who persist in it show they never truly rested on Christ (1 John 2:19). True believers may be confused and tempted, as the Galatians were, but God keeps his own (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29), and warnings like this one are among his means of keeping them. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Falling from grace here means abandoning the principle of grace, not a true believer being lost. That is why Paul can write verse 4 and verse 10 in the same breath.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that sinning makes you fall from grace. Grace is for sinners. Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more (Romans 5:20).

I am afraid this describes me. Does it? Ask what the verse actually describes: a person who is seeking to be justified by his own law-keeping and is at peace with that arrangement. Now ask whether that is you. If you are afraid because you know your record will not carry you, that fear is not the condition Paul is describing; it is the exact opposite of it. Nobody standing on his own performance is troubled by the news that performance will not do. A warning against a cliff is not a report that you have gone over it, and the people who read it most anxiously are almost always the ones furthest from the edge.

How would I know if I were trying to be justified by the law? Watch where your confidence goes when you think of standing before God. If you find yourself listing what you have done, how long you have been a Christian, how much you give, what you avoid, you are reaching for the rope instead of the boat. If you find yourself saying, nothing in my hands I bring, simply to the cross I cling, you are in grace. Most Christians drift between the two in a single week. The remedy is not to examine yourself harder but to look at Christ longer.

A change of footing. What the verse does require is a change of footing, and that is simple enough to do today. Not more effort. Less. Stop asking whether you have done enough to be received, and look at what was done for you, and stand there. That is all grace has ever asked of anybody. If it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works (Romans 11:6), and the righteousness Paul wanted was not his own but that which comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9).

In a sentence. You who are trying to be justified by the law have been alienated from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.

On a Tuesday. Falling from grace is not sinning; it is trying to earn God’s favour. Stay in grace. When you sin today, do not try to pay for it with a better tomorrow. Confess it, and rest again on the one who has already paid.

For worship. Grace is not a ledge we cling to by our fingernails. It is a place, a standing, a country, and its King is the one who holds us there. We have obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand (Romans 5:2), and the hand that brought us in is the hand that keeps us. The Shepherd who laid down his life for the sheep has said that no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he has never yet lost one the Father gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.

For through the Spirit, by faith. Having said what law-standing does, Paul says what the other position looks like, and the first word is emphatic in a way most English readers miss. He has just said you to the ones seeking justification by law. Now he says we ourselves: the pronoun is emphatic in the Greek, drawing a line down the middle of the room. There are two positions here, and Paul is telling the Galatians which side of the line he stands on and inviting them back over it. The Christian way is the Spirit, received by faith.

We ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness. Much of the sentence is about waiting. Eagerly wait is apekdechometha: to wait eagerly for a thing that is certainly coming and is not here yet. That is a striking word to use of righteousness, when Paul has spent three chapters insisting the believer is justified already. The hope of righteousness is the final verdict of acquittal at the judgement, the full and public revelation of our righteousness in Christ, and the day when we are finally and actually like him.

Already and not yet. Both are true, and holding them together is the whole balance of the Christian life. Believers are already justified (Romans 5:1): the verdict has been passed, and you are righteous in Christ now, today, with nothing outstanding. They wait confidently for that verdict to be publicly declared, and for the state that matches it, when the man you want to be and the man you are have at last become the same man. Every believer lives in the gap between those two, and the gap is uncomfortable, and it is not a sign that anything has gone wrong.

The legalist cannot wait. A legalist, by contrast, cannot wait. Waiting requires that the outcome be secure without your involvement, and a man whose standing depends on his own progress cannot afford to wait for anything; he has to be getting somewhere, visibly, or the whole structure wobbles. The gospel produces patient people because it has already settled the question they would otherwise spend their lives trying to answer.

For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything. Then verse 6, and it is one of the great summarising sentences of the New Testament. The first half is remarkable coming from Paul in this letter. He has fought circumcision for four chapters; you might expect him to say that being uncircumcised is what counts. He says neither does. Ethnic and religious markers are irrelevant to standing with God. The moment you make your uncircumcision a badge, you are playing the same game with the pieces reversed, and every generation of the church finds a way to do it, taking pride in the tradition it has rejected as thoroughly as its neighbours take pride in keeping it.

But only faith working through love. Four words, and they have been fought over for centuries, so it is worth being exact. The verb is energeō: operating, energised, at work. Faith is the living thing, and love is faith at work. True faith is never idle; it shows itself in love. Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone. A faith that produces no love is not a faith that needs supplementing. It is a report of something that was never there.

Where Christians differ: faith working through love. Roman Catholic teaching has used this phrase to argue that we are justified by faith formed by love, so that love is part of the ground of justification. Verdict: Paul says what counts is faith, and describes that faith as one that works through love. Love is the fruit of justifying faith, not part of its ground, and the grammar agrees: love is not what qualifies faith, it is what faith does. We are justified by faith alone, receiving Christ’s righteousness; the faith that receives Christ then works through love (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17; Westminster 11.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith without works can save. Dead faith is not saving faith (James 2:17–18), and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2). It means works are the fruit, not the root.

If love is the evidence, how much love is enough? That is the wrong question, and it is the question the Judaizers taught people to ask. Love is not the entrance fee; it is the sign of life. A newborn baby breathes weakly, but it breathes, and the doctor does not ask whether it breathes enough to be human. Look for direction, not quantity: is there a love for God and for his people that was not there before, and is it growing, however slowly? If it is, it is the Spirit’s work. If you are troubled by how little you love, bring that trouble to Christ, whose love for you does not depend on yours for him, and ask him to enlarge your heart.

Where to look. So the test is neither, have I done enough?, nor, do I believe the right things in the abstract? It is whether the trust you have placed in Christ is doing anything, and the place to look is not your religious activity but the person nearest you who is difficult to love. That is where faith shows whether it is alive, and it is a far more searching examination than any of the ones the Judaizers were offering.

In a sentence. For through the Spirit we eagerly await by faith the righteousness for which we hope. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. The only thing that counts is faith expressing itself through love.

On a Tuesday. Think of the one person in your home, work or church whom you find hardest to love. Do one concrete thing for their good this week, without telling anyone. That is not a way of earning God’s favour; it is faith, which already has God’s favour, getting to work.

For worship. The faith that justifies looks entirely away from itself to Christ, and finds there a righteousness already complete. And then, being alive, it turns round and loves, because it has been so loved. We wait for the hope of righteousness not as candidates nervously awaiting results, but as a bride waits for the wedding: certain of the day, eager for the Bridegroom, and already wearing the ring. The God who declared us righteous in Christ will one day make us everything his declaration says, and on that day the whole creation will see what his grace has done.

verseByVerse.quote: You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion is not from him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump.

You were running well. The metaphor is the stadium, and Paul uses it warmly. They started the Christian life well. He is not sneering at them. He is a coach watching a runner who had a good rhythm and a good line and was going to finish, and something happened.

Who hindered you from obeying the truth? The verb is enkoptō: to cut in, to block, as a runner cutting across another’s lane. Someone tripped them up. So Paul is not describing a runner who got tired or lost heart. Somebody stepped in front of him. And obeying the truth means believing and living the gospel: for Paul the truth is something you do as well as something you hold.

Who got in front of you? That is a more useful diagnosis than it first appears, because Christians who have gone backwards usually blame themselves for a failure of stamina, and it is often not that at all. Somebody cut in. A teacher, a book, a friend with strong opinions, a season under a ministry that made the gospel conditional. The question Paul asks is worth asking honestly of any cooled faith: not, why did I run out of energy?, but, who got in front of me, and when? Very often there is a date.

This persuasion is not from him who calls you. Then verse 8, and it is a quiet, devastating sentence. He does not say the teaching is unhelpful, or unbalanced, or that its advocates mean well. He says God, who called them by grace, is not the source of this new teaching. And notice how he identifies God: as him who calls you, present tense, still calling. The argument is: you know the voice that called you, because you have heard it. This is not that voice.

A test for ordinary believers. That gives a test that ordinary believers can actually use, and it is more reliable than assessing arguments. Does this teaching sound like the God who called you? Not, is it strict? God is often strict. But does it come to you the way he came to you? He came with a gift, to someone with nothing to offer, and the effect was relief. When a teaching arrives and its effect is that you feel measured, watched, and slightly behind, you may not be able to refute it. You can still recognise that it is not the voice that called you. My sheep hear my voice, Jesus said (John 10:27).

A little leaven leavens the whole lump. Then verse 9, a proverb. Everyone in that world had watched it happen. A pinch of sour dough goes into a large batch, and nothing appears to happen for hours, and then the whole mass has changed and there is no part of it that has not (1 Corinthians 5:6). Two things follow. First, quantity is irrelevant. The Judaizers were asking for one concession, and Paul’s point is that a gospel with a small condition attached is not mostly the gospel; given time, it is a different loaf entirely. Second, the change is invisible while it is happening. Nobody in a church that is losing the gospel can feel it going. The sermons remain biblical, the meetings continue, the language is unchanged, and what alters first is only the atmosphere: the quiet arrival of measurement into a room that used to be full of relief. That is why Paul is writing at this volume about what looks, to everyone in Galatia, like a modest adjustment. False teaching, though it starts small, spreads.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every small disagreement corrupts the church. It means adding to the gospel, even a little, is deadly.

How do I tell whether a teaching is leaven or just a different emphasis? Ask what it does to the gospel of free justification in Christ. Christians differ honestly on baptism, church government, the end times and much else, and those differences, important as they are, need not touch the heart. Leaven is different: it changes what makes a person right with God, or adds a condition to Christ, or quietly moves the weight from his work to yours. Ask: does this leave me resting wholly on Christ? Does it make grace more amazing or less? Does it fit with the plain teaching of Scripture, read as a whole? If a teaching makes Christ smaller and you larger, it is leaven, however small it looks.

In a sentence. You were running a good race. Who cut in on you to keep you from obeying the truth? That kind of persuasion does not come from the one who calls you. A little yeast works through the whole batch of dough.

On a Tuesday. Watch for small compromises in the gospel. They spread. If your own faith has cooled, look back and ask when it began, and what voice you were listening to then. Then go back to the voice that first called you: open the Gospels and listen to Christ again.

For worship. The God who called us is still calling, and his voice has not changed. He called Abraham out of Ur, Israel out of Egypt, the Galatians out of their idols, and us out of darkness into his marvellous light, and every time the call came with a gift in its hand. And the race we run is not a contest to win his favour but a course he has marked out, with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, waiting at the finish (Hebrews 12:1–2). He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) spreads through the whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!

I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view. After the leaven, a surprise. Nothing in the letter prepares you for that sentence. He has called them foolish, bewitched, severed from Christ, and now he says he is confident about them, and where that confidence rests is stated with precision: in the Lord. Not in their good sense, of which he has seen little, nor in the strength of his own arguments. Paul trusts that God will bring them back.

How to hold on to someone who is drifting. That is how a Christian holds on to somebody who is drifting, and it is worth learning, because the alternatives are both bad. You can be confident in the person, which is not faith but optimism, and it collapses on contact with facts. Or you can write them off, which is tidier and feels like realism. Paul does neither. He tells them the worst honestly and then declares his expectation that God will keep them, which is the only ground on which anyone has ever been kept, including him.

And the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is. Then the other half. The singular is interesting: a particular man, evidently, whose name Paul may not know, or a way of saying each one of them. God will judge the false teacher, however important. And notice what Paul does with him. He does not organise a campaign against him; he hands him over to God’s judgement and leaves him there. Whoever he is has a shrug in it: he will answer, and Paul does not need to know his name to be sure of it.

But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? Verse 11 lets slip what was being said about Paul. Somebody in Galatia had been claiming that Paul himself taught circumcision when it suited him (perhaps pointing to Timothy, or to his past as a circumcising Pharisee), and therefore that the Galatians were only being asked to do what the apostle really wanted. Paul’s answer is not a denial but a piece of evidence: look at my life. Nobody stones a man for preaching what everybody already accepts. If so, why do Jews still persecute him? The scars are the argument.

In that case the offense of the cross has been removed. And then the phrase that explains everything. The word is skandalon: the trigger of a trap, the stumbling block, the stone that trips a man. What offends is not the suffering; the world has always admired a martyr. It is what the cross says about the person looking at it: that he could not be saved by any other means, that his religion and his decency contributed nothing, that he had to be rescued like a criminal. Add circumcision, or any other requirement, and the offence drains away instantly, because now there is something for the man to do, and human pride is satisfied. A religion you can contribute to is a religion the world will tolerate. Paul says the persecution is the proof that the offence is still in his preaching. A gospel nobody is annoyed by has usually been adjusted. The gospel of grace always offends human pride.

What is the offence of the cross today? Much the same as then, though it wears modern clothes. People are offended to be told that they are sinners who cannot save themselves; that decent, religious and kind people need a Saviour as much as criminals do; that there is only one way to God, through a crucified Jew; and that their good works earn nothing. People will happily admire Jesus as a teacher or example. What they resist is being told they needed him to die for them. Do not soften those points to be liked. Explain them gently, with tears if need be, but leave the offence where God put it, because it is the same message that saves.

I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves! Then verse 12, and it is startling. It reads as a crude outburst until you know where the letter is going. Across Asia Minor, with its chief shrine at Pessinus in Galatia itself, the mother goddess Cybele was served by priests who castrated themselves in ecstatic worship. Readers in the region knew that cult. So Paul is not merely being coarse. He is saying: you want to cut flesh to be accepted by God? Then you already know what that religion looks like, because it is on your own doorstep. If the knife is the mechanism, why stop where Moses stopped? Take it to the shrine and finish the job, and become like pagan priests. It is the most cutting sentence he ever wrote, and it is aimed at showing the Galatians that the road they are on ends somewhere they have already seen. Strong words, showing how seriously Paul takes the danger.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may use crude insults freely. Paul’s language reflects the extreme danger to souls.

Is strong language ever right for me? Rarely, and with great care. Paul was an apostle writing under inspiration about wolves who were destroying a flock he had founded, and even here his target is the teachers, not the confused sheep. Elsewhere Scripture tells us to let no corrupting talk come out of our mouths (Ephesians 4:29) and to correct opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25). If you find you enjoy biting words, that is a sign to stop. Keep your strongest language for the dangers that most threaten souls, and even then speak it with sorrow, never with relish, and never against the people who are being misled.

In a sentence. Paul is confident in the Lord that you will take no other view. The one who is throwing you into confusion, whoever that may be, will have to pay the penalty. Brothers and sisters, if he is still preaching circumcision, why is he still being persecuted? In that case the offence of the cross has been abolished. As for those agitators, he wishes they would go the whole way and castrate themselves!

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you love who is drifting. Write down one sentence of confidence, not in them, but in the Lord about them, and pray it every day this week. And when you share the gospel, notice whether you are tempted to leave out the part that offends. Put it back.

For worship. Do not try to remove the offence of the cross; it is the very glory of God. The cross says that we could do nothing, and that God did everything. It says that the Judge stepped down from the bench and took the sentence himself. It says that the righteous died for the unrighteous to bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). To the proud it is a stumbling block and folly, but to those who are called, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). Far be it from us to boast except in that cross.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s bitter wish may allude to the priests of the goddess Cybele in that region, who castrated themselves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They were called to freedom, but they must not use it as an excuse for the flesh; instead they should serve one another in love. The whole law is summed up in one command, to love your neighbour as yourself. If they bite and devour one another, they will be destroyed by each other.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

The relation of law and love in Reformed ethics is exact. The law’s moral demands are not abolished for the believer; they are fulfilled, but from a different source and in a different direction. The law compels from outside and leaves the sinner exposed; love, produced by the Spirit, constrains from within and overflows. This is what the older divines meant by the law written on the heart (Jer. 31:33) — not a different law, but the same law internalised by the Spirit of adoption and obeyed as the expression of a heart that loves the God who gave everything, rather than as the price of his favour.

Verse 13 also settles the charge of antinomianism that has followed the doctrine of free grace since the first century. Paul concedes the danger frankly and then refuses the remedy his opponents wanted. That refusal is the test of whether a man has understood the gospel he preaches: it is easy to answer licence with law, and it undoes everything. And v. 15 exposes the mechanism by which a doctrine of performance destroys a congregation — once standing is earned, every other believer becomes a measurement, and the resulting suspicion has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were living out v. 15 while arguing about how to be holy, which is not an irony but a mechanism. The very community the Judaizers claimed to be perfecting by law-observance was tearing itself apart, and vv. 13–14 name the only thing that binds a church in the way rules never can.

Now:A church that makes the Christian life primarily about observable markers will always produce the same social weather: pride in those who meet the standard, shame in those who do not, comparison, and division. The cure v. 13 offers is not a new rule but service, given concretely to the person you are still disagreeing with.

verseByVerse.quote: For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

For you were called to freedom, brothers. Paul returns to where the chapter began. God called them into freedom. And now he faces the objection that has been waiting since verse 1, and that every preacher of grace has had put to him: if people are genuinely free, what is to stop them doing as they like?

Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. He does not dodge it. The word aphormē is military: a base of operations, a launching point, the staging ground from which an assault is launched. The flesh is sinful human nature. So the danger is real, and Paul names it plainly: your liberty can be occupied. The flesh will move into the space grace has cleared and use it as a forward position, and the reasoning it offers is always theologically impeccable. I am not under law. God has forgiven this already. Grace is greater than my sin. Every one of those sentences is true, and all three have been used to excuse things that wrecked a family.

No fence, but love. But watch what Paul does not do next. He has just diagnosed licence, and the obvious remedy is a fence: some law, reintroduced at the end of the letter, to keep freedom in bounds. He refuses. Having spent four chapters demolishing law as the ground of standing, he will not smuggle it back as the ground of behaviour. His answer to the flesh is not restriction. It is love.

But through love serve one another. And the verb is deliberately shocking: douleuete, from douleuō, to be a slave, the root of doulos. Be slaves to one another. Paul has spent the whole letter tearing the yoke off their shoulders, and the first thing he tells them to do with their freedom is to put themselves at each other’s disposal. Ironic and beautiful: freed from slavery to the law, believers become slaves of one another in love. True freedom is freedom to love.

Free lord, dutiful servant. That is the paradox at the centre of Christian liberty, and Luther put it exactly: a Christian is a perfectly free lord of all, subject to none, and a perfectly dutiful servant of all, subject to all. The two are not in tension, because the slavery Paul has been fighting is slavery to a system in order to be accepted, and this is bondage to a person because you already are. One is how you try to get standing. The other is what standing does.

For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Then verse 14, quoting Leviticus 19:18 (compare Romans 13:8–10). A reader is entitled to be puzzled. Paul has said the believer is not under the law, and here he quotes Leviticus as though it settles everything. The resolution is in the verb. He does not say the law is summarised in love, as if love were a convenient abridgement. He says it is fulfilled: filled full, brought to its intended completion. The law was never an arbitrary list; every commandment in it was describing what love looks like when it meets a particular situation. Do not steal is love meeting your neighbour’s property. Do not bear false witness is love meeting his reputation. So a man who genuinely loves is not evading the law. He is doing the thing the law was written to produce, not to be justified, but as its fruit, in the way that a man who loves his wife does not need a rule against reading her letters.

A higher standard, not a lower one. So the standard is higher and not lower. A code can be satisfied; you can reach the end of a list. As yourself has no end to reach. Nobody has ever gone to bed having loved his neighbour as much as he instinctively looks after himself.

So does the law still bind the believer? If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law (v. 18) means not under it as a covenant of works, a curse or the ground of our standing. It does not mean that God’s moral will has lapsed. The law still describes what love does: this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments (1 John 5:3). Love fulfils the law; it does not abolish it. The Spirit-led Christian does not need the law to make him acceptable, but he is glad of it as a description of the life the Spirit is producing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love replaces the commandments, so that we decide what love means. Love is defined by the commandments (Romans 13:9). A person who says, I am doing the loving thing, while breaking God’s commands about marriage, honesty or life, has redefined love to suit himself.

Does loving my neighbour as myself mean I must first learn to love myself? No. The command assumes that we already care for ourselves: we feed ourselves, protect ourselves, think about our own interests without being told to (Ephesians 5:29). It takes that instinct as the measure and turns it outward. The cure for a crushed sense of self is not self-love but being loved by God, which frees you to stop looking inward at all. And who is my neighbour? Jesus answered that with a Samaritan: whoever is in front of you and in need, even if he is not your kind (Luke 10:29–37).

In a sentence. You, brothers and sisters, were called to be free. But do not use your freedom to indulge the flesh; rather, serve one another humbly in love. For the entire law is fulfilled in keeping this one command: “Love your neighbour as yourself.”

On a Tuesday. Use your freedom today to serve someone in love. Pick a specific person and a specific service: the washing-up nobody wants to do, the visit you keep postponing, the message of encouragement, the hour given to a lonely neighbour. Do it as one set free, not as one paying a debt.

For worship. The freest man who ever lived wrapped a towel round his waist and washed his disciples’ feet. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He fulfilled the whole law, not by keeping a list, but by loving his Father with all his heart and his neighbours more than himself, all the way to the cross. Our freedom is the shape of his love, and every act of service we do is a small reflection of the one who served us first.

parallels.desc: you shall love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.

But if you bite and devour one another. The three verbs are all taken from animals, and they escalate. Bite is what a cornered creature does: a snap, a wound, not fatal. Devour is eating, taking a part of the other. Consumed, in the next clause, is the end of the process: nothing left. Paul is describing a sequence, like wild animals fighting, and he is describing it in a church. The controversy in Galatia had turned the churches into battlegrounds.

An argument about holiness. Which tells us something about the situation on the ground that the doctrinal argument alone would not. This was not a seminar. The Galatian congregations were tearing each other apart, and the argument they were tearing each other apart over was an argument about how to be holy. That combination is not an irony. It is a mechanism, and it is worth understanding, because it is still the commonest way a good church destroys itself.

How it works. Once standing before God is tied to performance, every other believer in the room becomes a measurement. If he keeps more than I do, he is a threat, and I must find the flaw that explains him. If he keeps less, he is a reassurance, and I need him to stay where he is. Neither of those is love, and both feel like discernment.
