Add a genuine doctrinal disagreement, and the whole thing has a righteous vocabulary to conduct itself in, so that people who are defending their own standing believe they are contending for the truth. Legalism often produces harsh criticism of others.

Watch out that you are not consumed by one another. Weigh Paul’s warning. He does not say the strong will eat the weak. He says you will be consumed by one another: everyone loses. Churches can destroy themselves through infighting, and conflicts of this kind have no winner. The party that prevails is left holding a smaller, colder, more suspicious congregation than the one it was fighting for.

What do you want to be true? Two practical things follow. The first is a test for a disagreement you are currently inside: ask what you want to be true about the other person. If you find you would be disappointed to discover he was right, or that his motives were good, then whatever the merits of your case, you are biting. The verse does not ask whether your position is correct. Paul obviously thought his was.

The cure is service. The second is the direction of the cure, and it is in the verse before. Paul does not answer biting with a rule against biting; he has just said, through love serve one another. The specific antidote to devouring a brother is serving him: deliberately, in some concrete way, while you still disagree with him. It is very hard to keep eating a man you are carrying something for. Pressing anger produces strife (Proverbs 30:33), and quarrels come from the passions at war within you (James 4:1–2); service starves them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean truth does not matter. Paul fights hard for it in this letter. It means believers must not attack each other with cruelty. You can contend for the faith without devouring the brother who is confused about it.

My church is already in a fight. What should I do? First, refuse to add to it: no gossip, no forwarding of messages, no recruiting to a side, no conversations about people that you would not have with them present. Second, if you have a grievance, take it directly and privately to the person concerned, and then if needed to the elders (Matthew 18:15–17). Third, pray for those you disagree with, by name, asking God to bless them. Fourth, look for a way to serve someone on the other side. And if the issue is a real matter of the gospel, speak plainly but without contempt. A church can survive disagreement; it rarely survives malice.

In a sentence. If you bite and devour each other, watch out or you will be destroyed by each other.

On a Tuesday. Think of the Christian you are most at odds with. Before you speak about them again, do something kind for them. Then, if you still need to disagree, disagree with them face to face.

For worship. The Good Shepherd did not bite and devour his flock; he let himself be devoured for them. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). He prayed for those who drove in the nails, and he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). The church is the people he bought at that price, and there is not one member of it whom he does not love. Every quarrel we lay down is an act of praise to the one who laid down his life to make us one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–26 — The Flesh and the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to walk by the Spirit, and they will not carry out the desires of the flesh, for the two are opposed and at war within them. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law. The works of the flesh are plain: sexual sin, impurity, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, envy, drunkenness and the like, and those who live this way will not inherit God’s kingdom. The Spirit produces a very different harvest: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, against which no law stands. Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions. Since they live by the Spirit, they should keep in step with him, and not become conceited, provoking or envying one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification and Vivification, and Why the Fight Is Evidence of Life

Reformed theology has always described the Christian life as two complementary movements: mortification, the putting to death of the flesh, which v. 24 states as something already done to every believer; and vivification, the coming alive to God, which v. 25 calls keeping in step with the Spirit. Neither is self-powered. The mortification is the application to daily life of what happened to the old self in Christ’s death (2:20); the vivification is the fruit of the Spirit’s indwelling. The believer does not produce either. He participates in both by faith.

The tension between v. 17 and v. 24 is resolved by the image itself. Crucifixion was chosen by Rome precisely because it was slow: a man nailed to a beam was mortally wounded, fixed, going nowhere — and still perfectly capable of shouting. That is the flesh in a believer. Its authority is broken and its outcome settled, and it will go on being audible until the body dies. Verse 21 must be read with the same care. Scripture never confuses a man who falls into a ditch with a man who lives in it, and the ache that makes a tender conscience afraid of that verse is itself the evidence the verse is not describing him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians needed to see that law and moral chaos were not the only two options, and vv. 16–18 give the third. Verse 20 would have been the most uncomfortable line in the letter read aloud in those congregations, since the middle of Paul’s list of fleshly works is a description of what was happening in the room. Verse 25 carries a piece of quiet artistry: stoichōmen, keep in step, is built on the same root as the stoicheia that had them in bondage in 4:3 and 4:9. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

Now:Walking by the Spirit (v. 16) is concrete rather than mystical: asking before the difficult conversation rather than after it, going where he speaks often enough to know his voice, and obeying the small prompt you would rather not have noticed. And v. 26 has a test anyone can run: what happens in you when good news is announced about the believer whose life is flourishing most visibly?

verseByVerse.quote: But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

But I say, walk by the Spirit. Here is Paul’s whole answer to the problem of Christian behaviour, and it is neither a law nor a technique. It is the answer to both legalism and licence. Walk is peripateite, from peripateō, a present imperative: go on walking, the ordinary word for how a man conducts his daily life, step by step. Not soar, not fight, not achieve. Walk. The Christian life at this point is being described in the plainest verb available. By the Spirit means depending on him, following his lead, relying on his power.

And you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Then the promise, and it is a promise and not a command. The Greek carries a strong double negative: you will certainly not carry out the flesh’s desires. Paul is not saying the desires will stop; he is saying they will not be carried out. And notice the order, which is the whole strategy of Christian holiness. He does not say, stop gratifying the flesh and then you will be able to walk by the Spirit. He says walk, and the other will follow. Sin is displaced far more often than it is defeated by direct assault, because a man staring at his temptation and gritting his teeth is still looking at it.

What the flesh is. Flesh here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God (for a fuller explanation of the word, see the note on Romans 8:3–4). It is not the body as such: several of the works of the flesh in vv. 19–21, like envy and rivalry, have nothing to do with the body.

For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh. Verse 17 is honest about the cost. This is a war within every believer, a settled state of war, and it should be said plainly, because young Christians often assume the conflict is evidence that something went wrong at their conversion. It is the reverse. Before conversion there was no war; the flesh had the field. The flesh still wants its way; the Spirit opposes it. The fight itself is a sign of life: there is now something in you that wants what God wants, and it will not be quiet.

For these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do. This phrase is easy to misread. Paul does not mean the believer is helpless, pulled in two directions with no way out. He means the two are locked in conflict, so that neither side gets its way unopposed. When the believer wants to do good, the flesh resists; when the flesh wants its way, the Spirit resists. You cannot simply drift into holiness, and you cannot sin with a quiet heart either. Notice the order in these verses: first the command and promise, walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the flesh (v. 16); then the explanation of why that command is needed, there is a war (v. 17). The conflict is real, but verse 16 has already told us which side wins when we walk by the Spirit. You are no longer a single, simple will that can do as it pleases. That is the price of having been rescued, and it will last as long as this life does.

What walking by the Spirit looks like. It is not a mystical state or waiting for a feeling. In practice it means: depending on the Spirit consciously, asking him for help rather than relying on willpower (Luke 11:13); filling the mind with his word, since the Spirit leads through what he has written, not apart from it (Colossians 3:16, compared with Ephesians 5:18); saying no to the flesh at the first stirring, not after a long negotiation (Romans 8:13); saying yes to the next step of obedience he shows you, even small ones; and staying close to God’s people and the means of grace, where he works. Walking is step by step: no single great experience settles it, but daily, ordinary dependence does. It is asking, before the difficult conversation rather than after it. It is obeying the small prompting of conscience, shaped by Scripture, that you would rather not have noticed. It is doing the next right thing in the strength of somebody else. None of that is exotic. It is what dependence looks like when it is spread across an ordinary week.

But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. Then verse 18 puts the alternative to the law where the chapter has been heading all along. Led is agō, as in Romans 8:14, and note the passive: led. The Judaizers offered a code to be kept; Paul offers a person to be followed. Those led by the Spirit are not under the law’s condemnation, nor under it as a system of control; they fulfil it from within. And a code, however holy, can only stand outside you and tell you what to do. The Spirit is inside, and he does not merely require the life. He produces it.

Does being led by the Spirit mean following inner voices and impressions? Not in the sense many people mean. In Romans 8:14 and here, being led by the Spirit is about the direction of a life, the Spirit leading God’s children away from the flesh and toward holiness, not a stream of private messages about which job to take. The Spirit speaks in Scripture, which he inspired and which is complete and sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). He does work in our hearts: convicting, comforting, bringing his word to mind, giving wisdom. But an impression is never to be treated as a new word from God, and anything that contradicts Scripture is not his leading. Test every prompting by the Bible.

Where Christians differ: sinless perfection. Some teach that believers can reach a state where the flesh is eradicated and they no longer sin. Verdict: Paul describes an ongoing war between flesh and Spirit in the believer. The Spirit gives real victory, and believers grow in holiness, but the flesh is not destroyed until glory (Romans 7:14–25; 1 John 1:8; Westminster 13.2). The Christian life is a fight, not a state of sinless rest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are helpless. The Spirit is stronger, and walking by him brings victory. He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. So Paul says, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are in conflict with each other, so that you are not to do whatever you want. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.

On a Tuesday. When you feel the pull of the flesh today, stop and pray: Holy Spirit, lead me. Then do not stand there arguing with the temptation. Turn your attention to something the Spirit loves: a verse you know, a person you can serve, a task you have been given. Walk away from the ditch by walking toward something.

For worship. The God who commands us to walk has come to walk with us. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation, who overshadowed the virgin, who raised Jesus from the dead, has taken up residence in ordinary believers, and he does not give up on them. He fights in us against everything that would destroy us, and he is not losing. The Father gave his Son for us and his Spirit to us, and between the cross behind us and the glory ahead, the Spirit walks every step of the road with us, until the war is over and the flesh is gone for ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature in its fallen state, set against God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Now the works of the flesh are evident. Before the list begins, two words are worth weighing. Evident is phanera: obvious, plain, on the surface. And works, erga: what the flesh produces. It is the same word Paul has used all through the letter for works of the law, and the echo is deliberate. Law-keeping and licence look like opposites, and Paul files them under the same heading, because both are things a man produces out of his own resources. Only the products differ. Fifteen are listed, in four groups.

Sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality. Sexual sin comes first. Sexual immorality (porneia) is the broad word for all sex outside marriage. Impurity (akatharsia) is moral uncleanness. Sensuality (aselgeia) is open, shameless indulgence: not merely indulgence, but indulgence that has stopped caring who sees.

Idolatry, sorcery. Then religion goes wrong. Sorcery translates pharmakeia, from which we get pharmacy: the ancient trade of potions, spells and drugs used to bend outcomes, common in Galatia. Both belong on a list of fleshly works because both are attempts to manage the divine: an idol is a god you can locate, and a spell is a result you can arrange.

Enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy. And then the long middle, which is where the reader should slow down. Eight sins of relationships, the largest group: enmity (hostility), strife (quarrelling), jealousy, fits of anger (outbursts of rage), rivalries (selfish ambition), dissensions (splits), divisions (factions, haireseis), envy. Eight items, more than half the catalogue, and every one of them is a sin of the church meeting rather than the tavern. This is not an accident. These were tearing the Galatian churches apart (v. 15), and Paul has put the sins of the respectable at the centre of his list of the works of the flesh. Respectable church people commit these. A congregation that would be horrified by verse 19 will often carry verse 20 as its ordinary weather.

Drunkenness, orgies. Sins of excess. Orgies (kōmoi) were wild partying, the drunken processions that ended festivals.

And things like these. The list is not complete. Paul is not writing a legal code. It is a portrait, not a schedule, and nobody can plead that his particular version is not itemised.

I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Then the warning, and it is one of the passages in the New Testament that most disturbs tender consciences. A believer reads the list, finds himself somewhere in it, and most honest Christians will find themselves in the middle section within the last month, and concludes that the door has closed. So read the verb carefully, because everything turns on it. Do is prassō, practise, in the present tense: those who go on doing them, whose lives are characterised by them, who have made their peace with them. Not the believer who falls and repents, but the one who continues in them without repentance (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). It is not a description of the sin you fought and lost this week and hated yourself for. There is a world of difference between a man who falls into a ditch and a man who lives in it, and Scripture never confuses them.

The morning after. Here is the test, and it is one anyone can run. What do you do the morning after? Not whether you sinned: you did, and so did everyone reading this. Whether the sin still grieves you, and whether you take it anywhere. A man in whom the Spirit lives cannot sin comfortably. The very ache that makes you afraid of this verse is the evidence the verse is not about you. Nobody who has stopped inheriting the kingdom is troubled by the thought of losing it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a single sin excludes a believer from the kingdom. It means a life ruled by the flesh shows a person is not ruled by the Spirit. And notice how Paul’s parallel list in Corinthians ends: and such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (1 Corinthians 6:11). The list describes what we were, not what we must stay.

I keep falling into the same sin, a sexual one. Am I one of those who practise it? The question to ask is not whether you have fallen again, but which side you are on in the fight. Are you at peace with it, defending it, planning for it? Or do you hate it, confess it, and keep fighting it, even after many defeats? The second is not the life Paul condemns; it is the war of verse 17. But do not settle for endless defeat. Bring it into the light with a mature Christian friend or pastor (James 5:16). Remove what feeds it: devices, places, habits. Ask for help, practical and spiritual. And each time you fall, go straight back to Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7, 9).

Is it sorcery to take medicine? No. The word described magic, potions and drugs used to manipulate spiritual powers, often with occult practices attached. Medicine used to heal is a gift of God; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. What the verse condemns today includes occult practices like fortune-telling, spells and seeking spirits, and the misuse of drugs to escape or to alter the mind in the way drunkenness does.

In a sentence. The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity and debauchery; idolatry and witchcraft; hatred, discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, dissensions, factions and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. Paul warns you, as he did before, that those who live like this will not inherit the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Look honestly at this list, especially the middle eight. Which one has been your ordinary weather this month? Name it to God, confess it specifically, and turn to Christ for cleansing. If it involves another person, put it right with them this week.

For worship. Every item on this list is a door to death, and Christ walked through every one of them for us, not as a sinner, but as the sin-bearer. He was made sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). The immoral, the idolatrous, the envious and the drunkards of Corinth and Galatia were washed in his blood and given his name, and the same fountain is open still. The kingdom these sins forfeit is the very kingdom he purchased for sinners, and he gives it freely to everyone who comes to him, turning from these things, with empty hands.
verseByVerse.note: “Sorcery” translates a word that also covered magic potions and drugs.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.

But the fruit of the Spirit. Note the change of word before anything else. The flesh has works; the Spirit has fruit. Works are manufactured: you decide, you exert, you produce. Fruit is grown, and it is grown by something the branch does not do. No apple was ever produced by an apple tree straining. Fruit grows naturally from life; the Spirit produces it as we abide in Christ (John 15:4–5).

One fruit, not nine. And note the singular. Not fruits, nine of them, to be collected like badges. One harvest with many flavours, one fruit with nine facets: a single character, which is finally the character of Christ himself, being formed in a person (4:19). The works of the flesh are many and fragmented; the fruit of the Spirit is one, a whole character. You do not choose patience this year and gentleness next. They come together because they are one life.

Is love. Love heads the list, as it must, since verse 14 has just said the whole law is fulfilled in it. Agapē is self-giving love, the love that seeks another’s good at its own cost. It comes first and is the root of the rest (1 Corinthians 13): joy is love rejoicing, peace is love resting, patience is love waiting, and so on down the list.

Joy, peace. Joy (chara) is gladness in God, and the New Testament’s joy is not the same thing as cheerfulness of temperament; it survives circumstances that ruin cheerfulness, because its ground is outside them. Peace (eirēnē) is wholeness: first peace with God, and then, as a consequence, the inward rest of a man who has stopped negotiating his standing, and harmony with others.

Patience, kindness, goodness. Then three that turn outward. Patience is makrothymia, literally long-tempered: long-suffering, a long fuse, specifically with people, bearing with them. It is the word used of God’s forbearance with us. Kindness (chrēstotēs) is gracious tenderness, not mere politeness but active usefulness to somebody. Goodness (agathōsynē) is active moral excellence and generosity: moral substance, the quality of a man who is the same when nobody is checking.

Faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. Then three that hold the rest together. Faithfulness (pistis) is reliability and loyalty: being where you said you would be, keeping your word when it costs. Gentleness is prautēs, meekness, and it is not weakness; in Greek it could be used of a powerful horse that had been broken to the bridle, so it is strength under control. And self-control (enkrateia), mastery over desires, comes last, which is a striking thing to find on a list of things the Spirit produces, since it is the one every self-help programme in the world sells. Paul says it is a fruit. You do not generate it. You receive it, and then you use it.

Against such things there is no law. A dry piece of understatement, and it lands the whole argument of the chapter. No law forbids these. The Judaizers were afraid that grace would produce lawlessness. Paul says: look at what the Spirit actually produces, and then find me the legislature that would want to prohibit any of it. There is no statute against being patient. The law was always aiming at this, and the Spirit is producing it without the law’s help. The Spirit-filled life more than fulfils the law. And the nine words, read slowly, are a portrait of Christ himself: no one has ever loved, rejoiced, rested, waited, served, kept faith, stooped and governed himself as he did.

How is the fruit of the Spirit different from the gifts of the Spirit? The fruit is character, the same in every believer and growing for a lifetime. The gifts are abilities for service, distributed differently, as the Spirit apportions to each one individually as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11). The fruit matters more. Paul says that without love the greatest gifts are nothing (1 Corinthians 13:2), and Jesus warns of people who prophesied and cast out demons in his name and were never his (Matthew 7:22–23). A church should prize holiness above gifting.

I see almost none of this in myself. Have I got the Spirit at all? This list is often used to wound, so three things should be said. First, fruit is slow, and it is seasonal, and nobody digs up a tree in March to check. Second, you are the worst-placed person in the world to assess it: ask the people who live with you, who will almost always report growth the man himself cannot see. And third, notice what the sentence does not say. It does not say the fruit of the diligent Christian. It says the fruit of the Spirit, and he is not slow, and he is not uncertain of the outcome, and the growing was never your department.

If I cannot produce the fruit, what do I actually do? You stay connected to the vine, and you cooperate with the gardener. Abide in Christ by trusting him and staying in his word (John 15:7). Pray specifically for the fruit you lack. Put yourself where growth happens: the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers. Pull up weeds when you see them, by confessing and turning from sin. And when an opportunity comes to exercise patience or kindness, take it, trusting the Spirit to give what he asks. Effort is not excluded; it is the effort of a branch staying in the vine, not of a branch trying to grow apples by itself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are passive. They must sow to the Spirit (6:8) and keep in step with him (v. 25). But the growth is his work.

In a sentence. But the fruit the Spirit produces is love, joy, peace, forbearance, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

On a Tuesday. Pick one fruit of the Spirit you most lack. Pray for it today, and look for one chance to show it. If it is patience, the chance will probably come in a queue or a traffic jam or a slow child at the door; when it comes, breathe a prayer and wait.

For worship. Read the nine words again and you will see a face. Love that went to the cross; joy set before him that carried him through it; peace he left to his friends on the night he was betrayed; patience with slow disciples; kindness to lepers and children; goodness that no one could convict of sin; faithfulness to his Father to the end; gentleness that would not break a bruised reed; self-control before Pilate, when twelve legions of angels were a word away. The Spirit is making us like him. What God began in Christ he is growing in us, and one day the harvest will be complete, and the Son will be the firstborn among many brothers.
verseByVerse.note: “Fruit” is singular: one harvest with many flavours.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

And those who belong to Christ Jesus. That is, all true believers. This is not an achievement of unusually consecrated Christians. It is a description of everyone who is his.

Have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. The tense is the thing to notice: have crucified, a past action, complete. Paul is not issuing an instruction here. He is stating what happened to every Christian, and stating it as a fact about them before it is a duty for them. United to Christ in his death, believers have put the flesh to death (2:20; Romans 6:6). At conversion they turned decisively against their sinful nature.

If it is dead, what has been fighting? This raises the obvious difficulty, and it is worth putting bluntly. Seven verses earlier Paul described a war going on inside the believer that keeps him from doing what he wants. Now he says the flesh has been crucified. If it is dead, what exactly has been fighting? The answer is in the image itself, and it is one of the most useful things in the chapter. Crucifixion was not a quick death. That was the point of it: Rome chose the method precisely because a man nailed to a beam could take days to die, and for the whole of that time he was mortally wounded, fixed in place, going nowhere, and still perfectly capable of shouting at people. Crucifixion was slow, painful and final. He was finished. He was not yet silent.

The noise of a dying man. That is the exact condition of the flesh in a believer, and it explains something that otherwise makes Christians despair. The old life has received a wound it will not survive; its authority is broken, it has been condemned, and its outcome is settled. But it is still audible, and it will go on being audible until the day the body dies. So the voice you hear on a bad Thursday is real, and it is loud, and it is not evidence that nothing happened to you. It is the noise of something that has been executed and has not yet stopped.

When did this happen? Paul has already told us: I have been crucified with Christ (2:20). It happened at the cross, and it became yours when you were united to him by faith. Which is why the sentence begins where it does: those who belong to Christ Jesus.

Relief in the order. There is real practical relief in that order. If crucifying the flesh were your project, every failure would mean the work was not done and would have to be started again, and the Christian life would be a series of restarts. Because it is Christ’s finished work applied to you, your failures are the noise of a dying man rather than the recovery of a victorious one. You are not trying to kill the flesh from scratch. You are refusing to take orders from something that is already condemned. And so believers continue to put it to death daily (Romans 8:13; Colossians 3:5): not to make the execution happen, but because it has.

How do I put the flesh to death in practice? Starve it and refuse it. Starve it by cutting off what feeds it: if a certain website, friendship, habit or late-night hour regularly leads you into sin, remove it, however drastic that seems (Matthew 5:29–30; Romans 13:14). Refuse it by saying no at the first stirring, and saying it in Christ’s name: this is not who I am now. Replace it with the opposite good: generosity for greed, thanksgiving for complaining, service for envy. And do it all by the Spirit (Romans 8:13), in prayer, in the company of other believers, and in the confidence that the flesh has already lost.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the flesh no longer troubles believers. Verse 17 shows it does. It means its power has been broken and its doom sealed.

In a sentence. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.

On a Tuesday. When the old voice shouts today, answer it out loud if you need to: you were nailed to the cross with Christ; I do not take orders from you. Then do the next good thing.

For worship. Which is worth a moment of sheer wonder. He was nailed to a beam so that the thing that had owned us could be nailed there with him. Everything in us that was in love with its own ruin was fastened to that wood in his body, and the sentence carried out on him was carried out on it, and it will never get down. Our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing (Romans 6:6). The flesh still shouts from the cross, but Christ has come down from it, risen, and we have risen with him.

verseByVerse.quote: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

If we live by the Spirit. The if is not a doubt. In the Greek it assumes the thing is true: since we live by the Spirit, and we do. The Spirit gives life to all believers. Paul is arguing from a fact to its consequence, and the shape of the argument is the shape of all New Testament ethics: this is what you are, therefore be it. He never asks a Christian to become something in order to qualify. He tells him what he is and then asks him to live like it. Being, the indicative, becomes command: you have the Spirit, so walk with him.

Let us also keep in step with the Spirit. Then a change of verb that is easy to miss but is the whole point. In verse 16 the word was walk, the ordinary word for daily conduct. Here Paul uses a different one: stoichōmen, from stoicheō, a military term for keeping rank, marching in line, holding formation, matching the step of the man beside you. Follow the Spirit’s lead step by step, in daily obedience, as soldiers follow the one ahead.

The word turned round. And here is the thing that makes the sentence remarkable, a piece of quiet artistry that runs right back through the letter. That verb is built on the same root as stoicheia, the word Paul used twice in chapter 4 for the elementary principles that had the Galatians in bondage (4:3, 9). He takes the word for the thing that enslaved them and turns it into the word for walking free with the Spirit. The Galatians had been in ranks before; they had marched to a calendar and a code. Paul does not tell them to stop marching. He tells them who sets the pace now.

A different formation. So Christian freedom is not the absence of order. It is a different formation, and the two distinctions that matter are these. Under the law you kept step with a system that could not help you keep it; now you keep step with a person who is himself the power to do it. And under the law the marching was how you tried to get your standing; now it is what your standing produces.

Ahead or behind. The practical force of keep in step is that it names two ways of getting it wrong, and most Christians are prone to one or the other. You can march ahead of him: running on your own energy, taking initiatives you were never given, driving a ministry or a decision at a pace nothing has been given to sustain, and calling the exhaustion faithfulness. Or you can lag behind: hearing the small thing you should do, agreeing with it, and not doing it, until the agreeing has quietly become a substitute for the doing. Neither is dramatic, and neither looks like rebellion. Both are simply being out of step, and the correction in each case is the same and is not complicated: find where he actually is, and be there. He is not marching away from you. He sets the pace at something a real person can sustain over a whole life, which is exactly what the law never did.

What it does not mean. It does not mean waiting for feelings or inner voices. The Spirit leads mainly through his word.

How do I know where the Spirit is leading in a decision, like a job or a move? Begin with what he has already said. Scripture settles the moral boundaries: if an option requires sin, it is not his leading. Within those boundaries, the Spirit leads by giving wisdom, so ask for it (James 1:5), think carefully, weigh your gifts and responsibilities, consider how each option affects your love for God, your family and your church, and seek counsel from mature believers (Proverbs 15:22). Then decide, and trust God’s providence with the outcome. You do not need a sign or an inner voice. Keeping in step is mostly about the next obedient step, and a wise decision made in faith is a step in step.

In a sentence. Since we live by the Spirit, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what is my next step of obedience to the Spirit today? Take it. If you have been running ahead, slow down and rest; if you have been lagging behind, do the thing you have been agreeing with and not doing.

For worship. The Spirit who gives us life does not shout orders from a distance. He marches beside us, and within us, at a pace we can keep. The Father planned our salvation, the Son accomplished it, and the Spirit applies it step by step, day by day, for a whole lifetime, and he is never impatient with a slow soldier. The words that once described our chains now describe our march, and the one who sets the pace is leading us home.
verseByVerse.note: “Keep in step” is a military word for marching in line.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

Let us not become conceited. It is a small verse, and it is doing a large job. It stands between the fruit of the Spirit and chapter 6’s instructions about restoring a brother caught in sin, and it is the hinge between them: here is what walking in step actually looks like in a room full of other people. Paul brings the whole soaring argument of the chapter down onto how you feel about the Christian sitting three seats away. The root is named first. Conceited translates kenodoxoi, from kenodoxos: empty-glory, vainglory, glory with nothing inside it. Not glory that is deserved, and not glory that is even real; a reputation held up by air, often pride in spiritual achievements. And the moment a man’s significance depends on something that hollow, he cannot leave other people alone, because the only way to maintain a comparative standing is comparatively.

Provoking one another. So the two symptoms follow, and Paul pairs them because they are the same disease at different altitudes. Provoking is prokaleomai: challenging, as to a fight. It is what the man ahead does: needling, making sure the gap is felt. Those who feel spiritually superior provoke others.

Envying one another. Envying is what the man behind does: resenting, watching, quietly hoping for a stumble. Those who feel inferior envy others. They look like opposites and they are identical: both are a person whose eyes are fixed on another believer rather than on Christ, and whose sense of himself is being calculated from the difference. Pride and envy are two sides of the same comparison. The Spirit frees us from both.

What performance manufactures. This is also exactly what a religion of performance manufactures, which is why the verse sits where it does. If standing before God is earned, then every other Christian is either a rival or a reassurance, and there is no third option. It is only when a man knows he was received with empty hands that another man’s gifts stop being a threat.

The test. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortably easy to run. Think of the believer whose ministry, family or reputation is flourishing most visibly in your circle. What happens in you when good news about him is announced? A flicker of something before the congratulation catches up is not a trivial fault of temperament. It is verse 26 with your name on it, and Paul puts it directly after nine words about the fruit of the Spirit for that reason: envy is the one thing that cannot coexist with love, joy and peace, because it needs somebody else to have less.

Look somewhere else. And the cure is not to try harder to be pleased. It is to look somewhere else. Empty glory is only attractive while it is the best glory in view. Set beside the real thing, the Son of God who had glory in full, laid it down, took the form of a slave and was executed for people who were arguing about rank (Philippians 2:3–7), the competition in the third row loses its grip, not because you have condemned it but because you have stopped finding it interesting. He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

Is it wrong to admire another Christian, or want to be like them? No. Paul himself says, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), and Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7). Admiration thanks God for another’s gifts and wants to grow in the same direction; envy resents them for having what you lack and is secretly glad when they stumble. The difference shows when they succeed: admiration rejoices, envy aches. If you notice the ache, confess it, and then thank God aloud for the very thing you envied. That is how the Spirit turns envy into love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we may not encourage one another to good works (Hebrews 10:24). It means no competing.

In a sentence. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying each other.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing yourself with other Christians. Neither look down nor look up enviously. Look to Christ. Then pick the person you most often compare yourself with, and pray for their blessing by name, specifically, for the thing you most envy or most look down on.

For worship. There is only one glory that is not empty, and it belongs to the one who emptied himself. He had no need to provoke anyone, because he had nothing to prove, and no reason to envy anyone, because all things were his. Yet he took the lowest place, and God has highly exalted him and given him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9). In his presence our little rivalries look like children quarrelling over pebbles at the foot of a mountain. To him be glory, now and for ever; and in him we have all the glory we will ever need.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.<sup>2</sup>Look: I, Paul, say to you that if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you.<sup>3</sup>I testify again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is obligated to keep the whole law.<sup>4</sup>You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.<sup>5</sup>For through the Spirit, by faith, we ourselves eagerly wait for the hope of righteousness.<sup>6</sup>For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love.<sup>7</sup>You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth?<sup>8</sup>This persuasion is not from him who calls you.<sup>9</sup>A little leaven leavens the whole lump.<sup>10</sup>I have confidence in the Lord that you will take no other view, and the one who is troubling you will bear the penalty, whoever he is.<sup>11</sup>But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the offense of the cross has been removed.<sup>12</sup>I wish those who unsettle you would emasculate themselves!<sup>13</sup>For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another.<sup>14</sup>For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”<sup>15</sup>But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.<sup>16</sup>But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.<sup>17</sup>For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do.<sup>18</sup>But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.<sup>19</sup>Now the works of the flesh are evident: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality,<sup>20</sup>idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions,<sup>21</sup>envy, drunkenness, orgies, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.<sup>22</sup>But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,<sup>23</sup>gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law.<sup>24</sup>And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.<sup>25</sup>If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.<sup>26</sup>Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

6.title: Boasting Only in the Cross: The New Creation and the Community of Grace
6.overview:
The letter’s final chapter moves from the Spirit’s inner work to its outward expression in the community of faith. The freedom of the gospel, Paul has shown, is not moral permissiveness; it is the freedom that produces love, and love expresses itself in the concrete practices of the community. Chapter 6 describes what the community shaped by the gospel looks like: it bears burdens, restores the fallen gently, gives generously, sows to the Spirit, and refuses to grow weary in doing good.

The chapter reaches its climax in Paul’s autographic conclusion (vv. 11–18), where he returns one final time to the contrast that has driven the entire letter. The Judaizers boast in their circumcision program; they want to make a good showing in the flesh, to avoid persecution for the cross. Paul boasts in nothing except the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ — the event that crucified the world to him and him to the world. And this cross has created something radically new: not merely reformed Judaism, not a hybrid of law and grace, but a new creation. In the new creation, “neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” The old categories — the categories by which the Judaizers were demanding conformity — have been abolished. What remains is the new creation in Christ, the Israel of God, the community of those who walk by the rule of the cross.

The letter ends as it began: with the gospel. Paul opened with grace and peace; he closes with “grace be with your spirit, brothers.” He opened with astonishment that they were deserting grace; he closes with the reminder that grace is still there, still sufficient, still the only ground on which any person, anywhere, stands before God. Galatians is, from first to last, a letter about grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul takes six chapters of doctrine and puts them to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life. A brother caught in any transgression is to be restored — the word for mending a net or setting a bone — in a spirit of gentleness, by people who keep watch on themselves (v. 1). Verse 2 calls this bearing one another’s burdens and so fulfilling the law of Christ, which Paul has already defined as love (5:14). Verses 3–5 explain why restoration goes wrong: self-deception (v. 3), a verdict reached by comparison (v. 4), and forgetting that each will carry his own load on the day of account (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as a Community of Restoration

The Reformed tradition has never regarded the church as merely a preaching station but as a communion of saints — a body committed to mutual care, discipline and restoration. Verse 1 is the practical expression of the justification theology of the whole letter. We deal gently with a failing brother because we know we stand only by grace; the man who forgets his own proneness to sin will always be a prosecutor, and the man who remembers it will be a restorer. Gentleness without truth produces sentimentality, and truth without gentleness produces further fracture. Both are failures of the same verse.

Verses 2 and 5 together give the balance that keeps a church healthy, and both errors are recognisable. What is crushing a man, others are commanded to help carry; what is properly his own — his obedience, his repentance, his answer at the last day — nobody can carry for him, and pretending otherwise is not kindness. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him and calls it strength, and the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church or his spouse and calls it fellowship.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatian congregations were biting and devouring one another (5:15). Freedom had evidently been taken by some as licence, and the response of others was condemnation rather than restoration. Verse 1 corrects both errors at once, and v. 3 names what was fuelling the second: men who thought they were something. Verse 4 answers the comparison culture that ends chapter 5 in provoking and envying.

Now:Verse 2 puts a question that a warm and orthodox church can still fail: whose weight are you actually under — not whom you pray for, which costs very little, but whose burden has cost you a Saturday or money you had other plans for? And v. 4 is uncomfortably clarifying: when you last felt good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work or about somebody else’s?

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.

Meaning first. Galatians 6 shows what walking by the Spirit looks like in the church, and then sums up the whole letter. First, the Spirit-led community restores those who fall, gently and humbly, and carries one another’s burdens, while each person takes responsibility for his own conduct (vv. 1–5). Second, believers should support their teachers, and remember that God is not mocked: what we sow we will reap, corruption from the flesh or eternal life from the Spirit; so let us not grow weary of doing good, especially to fellow believers (vv. 6–10). Finally, Paul takes the pen and writes in large letters. The false teachers want circumcision so that they can avoid persecution and boast in others’ flesh. Paul will boast only in the cross of Christ, by which the world is crucified to him. What matters is not circumcision but a new creation. Peace and mercy on all who walk by this rule, the Israel of God. Let no one trouble him further; he bears the marks of Jesus on his body (vv. 11–18). The letter that began with grace ends with grace, and the last thing it holds up is a cross.

Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression. Paul has spent five chapters on doctrine, and the first thing he does with it is put it to work on the hardest situation in ordinary church life: what to do about a Christian who has fallen. The verb is passive, prolēmphthē, from prolambanō: overtaken, caught out, surprised by it. It may mean caught in the act, or overtaken by sin before he realised. The picture is not of a man who sat down and planned his rebellion but of one who was walking along and was ambushed. That does not make the sin smaller; Paul calls it a transgression (paraptōma), a false step, a slip, and any sin will do. It does change the posture you approach him in. You are looking at a casualty, not a defector.

You who are spiritual. Who qualifies? Not an elite tier of believers: Paul has just spent a chapter saying every Christian lives by the Spirit and should keep in step with him (5:16, 25). The spiritual are simply those actually walking in step today, those mature enough to help. But there is an edge in it, because the Galatians were full of people who thought themselves advanced, and Paul is quietly saying: if you are so spiritual, here is the job.

Should restore him. Restore is katartizete, from katartizō, and it is a lovely word. It is used of mending torn nets (Matthew 4:21) and, in medical writing, of setting a broken bone. Both pictures teach the same thing. Nobody sets a bone carelessly, and nobody sets one by shouting at it. It requires that you get close, that you know what you are doing, that you cause pain deliberately and only as much as the job needs, and that the entire object is a limb that works again. A surgeon who enjoyed the pain would be struck off. The goal is restoration, not punishment or exposure.

In a spirit of gentleness. The word is prautēs, and it appeared four verses ago in the fruit of the Spirit (5:23). That is not an accident. Paul has said what the Spirit produces, and now he shows you the room where it is needed most. Gentleness is not softness about the sin; it is strength under control, the broken horse rather than the tame one. Not harshly, not with superiority.

Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted. Then the safeguard, and the grammar shifts to make it land: keep watch on yourself is singular, suddenly, in a sentence full of plurals. Paul turns from the church to the individual doing the restoring and speaks to him alone. Humility: you could fall too. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Corinthians 10:12).

The real danger. Take that seriously, because the danger is real and it is not the obvious one. The temptation in a restoration is rarely to commit the same sin. It is to enjoy the position: to find that being the one who is well is unexpectedly pleasant, to relay the details as a prayer request, to feel a quiet firmness of ground under you that you did not have last week. That is a worse condition than the one you came to mend, and it is invisible to the man in it.

The practical shape of it. Go, rather than discuss him. Go having asked honestly whether you would want this conversation conducted on you the way you are about to conduct it. Say the true thing plainly, because gentleness that will not name the sin is not gentleness but cowardice wearing its coat. And go knowing that the only thing separating you from him is grace you did not generate. A man who has really grasped the first five chapters of this letter cannot be a prosecutor. He has read the charge sheet with his own name on it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring sin or pretending it does not matter. It means dealing with it in a gentle, restoring way.

And if the person will not be restored? Then the gentleness does not give way to indifference. Jesus lays out the steps: go privately, then with one or two others, then to the church (Matthew 18:15–17). Where someone who calls himself a believer persists in serious sin without repentance, the church must act (1 Corinthians 5:11–13), always with the aim of bringing him back.

What if the sin is abuse, or a crime? Then gentleness toward the sinner must never mean danger for the victim. Restoration in this verse is about a person’s relationship with God and the church; it does not cancel the duty to protect the vulnerable or to report a crime to the authorities, whom God has appointed to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4). Abuse is never to be hushed up, minimised or handled privately to protect a reputation, and no victim should be pressed to reconcile with an abuser or to stay in danger. The church can pray for a repentant offender and seek his good, while keeping him well away from those he harmed and from positions of trust.

Does being restored mean being given back the position he had? Not necessarily. Restoration means being brought back to repentance, forgiveness and fellowship: welcomed at the Lord’s Table, loved, no longer treated as an outsider. That should be full and warm. But trust, and especially leadership, is a separate matter. Scripture sets qualifications for elders, including being above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2), and a man who has gravely fallen may be fully forgiven and still rightly not hold office again, or only after long proof. Forgiveness is a gift; trust is rebuilt.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, if someone is caught in a sin, you who live by the Spirit should restore that person gently. But watch yourselves, or you also may be tempted.

On a Tuesday. Is there a fallen brother or sister you know? Go gently, aiming to restore. And keep watch over your own heart. Before you speak to them, pray for them by name, and confess to God the sin in yourself that is most like theirs.

For worship. This is what Christ did for us. He did not wait for us to climb back; he came to where we had fallen. He restored Peter by a charcoal fire, after three denials, with three questions and no lecture (John 21:15–17). He is the Physician who sets broken bones without breaking the spirit, the Shepherd who carries the stray home on his shoulders rejoicing (Luke 15:5). A bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3). Every gentle restoration in the church is a small picture of the great one: the Holy One stooping to mend sinners, and never once regretting it.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

Bear one another’s burdens. Bear is bastazete, a present imperative: go on carrying, as a habit. And the noun is barē: a weight, something heavy, the word for a load that presses a man down. Paul is not talking about minor inconveniences. He means the things that are genuinely too much for one person: trials, temptations, grief, sins, troubles. A marriage that is failing, a diagnosis, a son who has stopped speaking to his parents, the particular sin from the verse before that a man cannot get free of on his own. Christians help carry each other’s loads.

Restoring is burden-bearing. And notice how the two verses sit together. Verse 1 says restore the fallen; verse 2 says carry each other’s weight. Paul evidently thinks these are the same activity. Dealing with somebody’s sin is not an alternative to bearing his burden. It is bearing his burden, if it is done as verse 1 describes it.

And so fulfill the law of Christ. Then the phrase that startles. Paul has spent five chapters saying that the believer is not under law, and here, at the end, he uses the word positively and attaches Christ’s name to it. He is not smuggling the old system back in through the last door. The law of Christ is not a replacement code with new clauses; he has already said what it is. The whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour as yourself (5:14), and the Lord himself gave it as a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you (John 13:34; compare 1 Corinthians 9:21). Not the law of Moses, which the Galatians were tempted to take on, but Christ’s law of love, defined not by a list but by a life. And the standard is no longer only as you love yourself, but as I have loved you, which is a good deal more expensive.

Why his name is on it. There is a deeper reason, which turns the whole verse from an instruction into something better. Christ did not merely legislate burden-bearing. He is the one who bore the burden nobody else could lift: surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4). Christ bore our heaviest burden; we bear one another’s. When a Christian takes the weight of another man’s failure onto his own shoulders, he is not obeying a rule. He is doing, in miniature and at infinite distance, the thing that was done for him at Calvary.

Whose weight are you under? That makes the practical question quite specific, and it is worth answering rather than admiring. Whose weight are you actually under at the moment? Not who do you pray for: praying matters greatly, but it can be done entirely in your own house. Whose burden has cost you a Saturday, or money you had other plans for, or a friendship that got harder because you told the truth inside it? A church can be doctrinally immaculate, warm on a Sunday, and carrying nothing at all, because burden-bearing is invisible and voluntary and nobody ever notices its absence.

It will not be reciprocal. And it will not always even out, which is the last thing to say. Paul writes one another’s, and in a healthy church it evens out over years. But it does not even out on any given Tuesday, and the man who keeps accounts will not last. You carry, and sometimes you are carried, and the ledger between you was closed at the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should do for others what they should do themselves (v. 5). It means sharing burdens too heavy for one.

I am the one with the burden, and I find it hard to ask for help. What should I do? Ask anyway, because the command assumes there will be burdens to carry, and someone has to let them be carried. Pride often hides as independence: I do not want to be a nuisance. But refusing help denies others the chance to obey Christ, and leaves you crushed under a weight God never meant you to carry alone. Start small: tell one trusted believer the truth about what is happening. Say plainly what would help: a meal, a lift, someone to sit with you, someone to pray with you weekly. And if your burden is a sin you cannot break, tell a mature Christian; confession to one another is a means of healing (James 5:16).

In a sentence. Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfil the law of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Name one person in your church who is carrying something heavy. Do one concrete thing this week that costs you something to help carry it: an hour, a meal, a lift to the hospital, a phone call you have been putting off.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation (Psalm 68:19). He carried the weight of the world’s sin up a hill on his back, and the sorrows of every one of his people he has carried in his heart. He invites the weary and heavy-laden to come to him for rest, and he has never yet sent anyone away. The law of Christ is simply Christ’s own life poured into his people: the Burden-Bearer making burden-bearers, so that the church becomes a family where no one has to carry everything alone.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. For each will have to bear his own load.

For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Three verses that look like scattered proverbs, and are in fact a single argument about why restoration goes wrong. The problem is not technique. It is self-assessment. Paul is describing the exact frame of mind that makes a man unfit for verse 1. Pride prevents burden-bearing: those who think themselves superior will not stoop to help. Note that he does not say such a man deceives his neighbour, although he probably does. He deceives himself: the verb is one of leading your own mind astray. This is the peculiar quality of spiritual pride: it is the one sin that blinds you specifically to itself. A man knows when he has lost his temper. Nobody has ever thought, this morning I am inflated.

When he is nothing. That sounds crushing until you remember what the letter has established. Paul is not saying you are worthless; he has spent two chapters telling these people they are sons and heirs of God. He means you are nothing on your own account. Everything you have that is worth having came in as a gift. What do you have that you did not receive (1 Corinthians 4:7)? A man who forgets that has mistaken a delivery for an achievement.

But let each one test his own work. Then the remedy, in verse 4. The word is dokimazetō, from dokimazō, the term for assaying metal: putting it in the fire to find what it actually is rather than what it looks like. And notice the object: his own work. Examine your own life, not others’. That is the whole point. The Galatians were measuring themselves against one another, which is why the chapter before ends with provoking and envying (5:26).

And then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor. The result is stated oddly and repays attention. Paul is not endorsing self-congratulation. He is making a point about where the measurement comes from. A man who has assayed his own work has a real, if modest, sense of what God has actually given him to do and whether he is doing it, and any satisfaction comes from God’s work in his own life. A man who has measured himself against his neighbour has nothing at all, because his verdict depends entirely on who happens to be standing next to him, and it will change when the neighbour changes.

Arithmetic on other people. Run the test and it is uncomfortably clarifying. When you last felt reasonably good about your Christian life, was that a judgement about your work, or about somebody else’s? And when you last felt like a failure, the same question. Almost all of both feelings, for most people, most of the time, is arithmetic performed on other people.

For each will have to bear his own load. Then verse 5, and the reader stops, because it looks like a flat contradiction of verse 2. Bear one another’s burdens, and now each will have to bear his own load. Which is it? Two things resolve it. First, the words are different. A burden in verse 2 is barē, a crushing weight, the thing a man cannot carry alone. A load in verse 5 is phortion, the word for a soldier’s pack or a ship’s cargo: an assignment, the normal personal load each must carry, properly proportioned to the one carrying it. It is the very word the Lord uses when he says my burden is light (Matthew 11:30). Second, the tense. Verse 2 is a present imperative about now; verse 5 is a future: will have to bear. Paul is looking ahead to the day when each of us gives his own account (Romans 14:12), and no one else can stand in the queue for us.

Two errors. So the two verses are not in tension at all; they divide the world sensibly. Help with crushing burdens; carry your own responsibilities. What is crushing you, others are commanded to help carry. What is properly yours, your own obedience, your own repentance, your own answer at the last day, nobody can carry, and it is not a kindness to pretend otherwise. Both errors are common and both are recognisable. There is the Christian who will not let anyone near a weight that is breaking him, and calls it strength. And there is the Christian who has quietly transferred his own pack to his church, his counsellor or his spouse, and calls it fellowship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should never take pleasure in what God has done through us. It means do not measure yourself by others.

How do I actually test my own work? Hold it up to God’s word and God’s calling, not to other people. Ask: what has God given me to do, in my family, my work, my church, my neighbourhood? Am I doing it faithfully, with love, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23)? Where have I been lazy, proud or unkind? Where has God plainly helped me grow? Write the answers down if it helps, and talk them over with a wise friend who will be honest. Then thank God for the good, confess the bad, and get on with the next task. The aim is not a score but faithfulness.

In a sentence. If anyone thinks they are something when they are not, they deceive themselves. Each one should test their own actions. Then they can take pride in themselves alone, without comparing themselves to someone else, for each one should carry their own load.

On a Tuesday. Examine your own work today, not your neighbour’s. Carry your own load faithfully. Catch yourself the next time you start measuring yourself against another Christian, and turn the thought into a question about your own calling instead.

For worship. There is only one person who ever was truly something and made himself nothing. He who was in the form of God did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself (Philippians 2:6–7), and carried not only his own load but ours. Because he did, the day of account holds no terror for those in him: we shall each give our account, and the Judge will be the one who bore our sins. Every gift we have is from his hand, and every good work he will one day praise as though it were ours.
verseByVerse.note: A “burden” in verse 2 is a crushing weight; a “load” in verse 5 is one’s own pack.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verse 6 arrives without preliminaries and it is about money: let the one taught share all good things with the one who teaches. The verb is koinōneitō, from the word for fellowship, which tells you Paul did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Note also who is instructed — congregations to give, not teachers to raise support. The reversal has done real damage, because a man who must ask for his own living finds it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said one.

Verse 7 hardens the tone. God is not mocked uses a verb built on the word for the nose: nobody sneers at God and gets away with it. The farming principle that follows carries three certainties every agricultural town understood — you reap what you sowed, more than you sowed, and later than you sowed. It is the third that deceives people, because the gap is long enough to make the connection look unreal. Verse 8 names the two fields, and corruption is phthoran, decay: the flesh pays out not usually in catastrophe but in decomposition. The promise of eternal life to those who sow to the Spirit is not wages — six chapters forbid that — but the full growth of a life that was given.

Verse 9 assumes weariness rather than forbidding it, and Paul includes himself in the us. The one condition attached to the harvest is not achievement but persistence: if we do not give up. Verse 10 turns the weariness outward. As we have opportunity uses the same word as the season in v. 9, so the sowing season is now — which disposes of the commonest evasion, since it means while there is time, not when it is convenient. Doing good to everyone forbids the church turned inward; especially to the household of faith forbids a general benevolence that never reaches the believer two streets away.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Harvest as the Motive of Present Faithfulness

Reformed ethics has always read present obedience in the light of a future harvest, and vv. 7–9 are where Paul states it most plainly. The believer does not do good in order to earn the harvest; the harvest is secured by grace, and this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing a man sows can purchase eternal life. But the harvest is real and the reaping is certain, and the knowledge of it sustains present faithfulness. That is the farmer’s wisdom applied to the Christian life, not works-righteousness.

Verse 8 must be read in the terms already set, or it will contradict the letter. What it describes is a direction of life: the seed a man scatters shows which field he believes he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. And v. 6 grounds the support of gospel ministry in something older than church order — the Levites had no land and Israel ate with them, and Paul states the principle elsewhere as the labourer deserving his wages (1 Cor. 9:11; 1 Tim. 5:17–18), which is the Lord’s own saying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Galatians were weary — theologically confused, socially fragmented, and without Paul. The Judaizers’ programme was more structured and far more socially comfortable, and drifting toward it would have ended the trouble. Verse 9 is aimed exactly there: the harvest is coming, do not walk off the field. And v. 6 was not incidental either, since nothing in a congregation's life is a more exact readout of what its people actually believe than what happens to their money.

Now:Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, which is why v. 8 so rarely frightens anyone into faithfulness; and v. 9 belongs to named people at the end of their strength, to whom Paul offers not encouragement about their prospects but a fact about the universe.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.

Let the one who is taught the word. After the burdens and the boasting, money, and it arrives without any preliminaries at all. Taught is katēcheō, to instruct, from which we get catechism: those who receive regular teaching from God’s word.

Share all good things with the one who teaches. The word for share is koinōneitō, from koinōneō, the family of koinōnia, fellowship, partnership. That is the term the New Testament uses for the deepest communion of the church, and Paul uses it here of supporting the teacher, which tells you he did not regard the subject as a lower order of thing. Money is fellowship in its most testable form. And all good things is broad: not only money but food, hospitality, the ordinary provisions a household can share, and perhaps also encouragement and spiritual partnership.

Who is instructed. Notice who is told to act. Paul does not tell teachers to raise support; he tells congregations to give it. That is the healthy direction, and the reversal of it has done a great deal of damage. A man who must ask for his own living will find it very hard to say the unwelcome thing, and this letter exists because somebody said an extremely unwelcome thing.

Not a novelty. The principle is stated more fully elsewhere: if we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? (1 Corinthians 9:11, 14). And the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18), which is Paul quoting the Lord. So the teaching is consistent across his letters and it is not new; the Levites had no land, and Israel ate with them.

Why here? Because it is the first thing Paul thinks of after burden-bearing, and because of what comes next. Verse 7 begins, do not be deceived: God is not mocked, and the sowing and reaping that follows has as its immediate setting what a congregation does with its money. Nothing in church life is a more exact readout of what people actually believe.

Paul’s own freedom. And a word to the man for whom this is not an abstract question. Paul did not always take money; he made tents in Corinth rather than be a burden, and made it his boast to preach free of charge (1 Corinthians 9:15–18). So this is not a rule that a paid ministry is the only faithful shape. It is an instruction to the congregation, and the congregation is not permitted to use the apostle’s freedom as an excuse. He chose to go without. He never once said the teacher was not owed.

What decides your giving? Then the searching part, which is what makes this more than church administration. Ask what your giving is actually being decided by. Most Christians give from what is left, which means the teaching of the word is funded by the residue of a lifestyle that was designed without reference to it. Paul’s word is share: not tip, not subsidise, not fund from surplus. It assumes a common life in which what one has is available to the other, and that is a considerably more disturbing idea than a percentage.

What it does not mean. It does not mean teachers should demand support or preach for money. It means those who benefit should support them gladly. Elders are to be not greedy for gain (1 Peter 5:2), and a teacher who makes money the point has disqualified himself.

Does this mean I must give a tenth? The New Testament does not lay down a fixed percentage for Christians; it calls for giving that is regular, proportionate, generous and cheerful (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Christians differ on whether the tithe still binds, and many find it a wise starting place. Whatever your view, the question is not how little you can give but how gladly you can share. Begin by giving first, not last, from each pay; support your own church and those who teach you; and let your giving grow as God provides. Christ, though he was rich, became poor for your sake (2 Corinthians 8:9).

In a sentence. Nevertheless, the one who receives instruction in the word should share all good things with their instructor.

On a Tuesday. Thank God by name for those who teach you his word. Then look at your giving and ask whether it is a share or a leftover. And do something this week for your pastor or teacher beyond money: a note of specific thanks for something you learned, a meal, a promise to pray for him.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest has given his church teachers, and every one of them is a gift from the ascended Christ (Ephesians 4:11). He who had nowhere to lay his head was fed by women who provided for him out of their means (Luke 8:3), and he counted every loaf as love. The God who feeds the sparrows feeds his servants through his people, and turns every gift into fellowship. All good things come from him, and when we share them, we are only passing on his generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.

Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. The tone hardens without warning. And the verb is worth seeing: myktērizetai, from myktērizō, comes from the word for the nose, and it means to turn your nose up at someone, to sneer. Paul says God does not get sneered at, and the sense is not chiefly that he takes offence but that nobody gets away with it. No one can outwit God or ignore his laws without consequence. You may treat him as a system to be worked around; the treatment simply does not succeed.

For whatever one sows, that will he also reap. The picture is a farmer, and it is a universal principle (Job 4:8; Proverbs 22:8; Hosea 8:7). Plant wheat, get wheat. Plant weeds, get weeds. And it carries three certainties that everyone in an agricultural town understood without being told. You reap what you sow: the field returns the kind of thing that went into it, and no farmer has ever been surprised by the species of his own crop.
