You reap more than you sow, which is the entire point of farming and cuts both ways: a handful of seed returns a sheaf, and so does a handful of the other thing. And you reap later than you sow, which is the certainty that deceives people, because the gap between the sowing and the harvest is long enough to make a man think the connection is not real.

The gap. That gap is what verse 7 is aimed at. Nobody sneers at God while the harvest is coming in. The sneer happens in month four, when nothing has visibly followed and the whole warning seems overwrought. Paul’s answer is not that judgement is coming quickly. It is that the ground is keeping the account whether or not anyone is watching it.

For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. Then verse 8 names the two fields. Sowing to the flesh is investing your life, time, money and energy in sinful desires (5:19–21). The harvest is phthora: corruption, decay, the process by which a thing rots, ending in ruin and eternal destruction. That is a precise description rather than a mere threat. The flesh does not only pay out in catastrophe; it pays out in decomposition: a marriage that goes quietly hollow, an appetite that needs more each year to do the same work, a conscience that stops registering, a man in his sixties who cannot say what he built. Nothing dramatic ever happened. It simply went off. And at the end, the decay is not merely of a life but of a soul.

But the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life. Sowing to the Spirit is investing in what pleases the Spirit: prayer, Scripture, worship, love, service. The harvest is eternal life. And here a guard is needed, because the sentence can be read as wages for services rendered, which would contradict the entire letter.

Where Christians differ: is eternal life earned by sowing? Some take this verse to mean salvation is a reward for good living. Verdict: Eternal life is God’s free gift in Christ (Romans 6:23), received by faith (the whole message of Galatians). But the life of faith shows itself in sowing to the Spirit, and that life leads to its harvest. Sowing to the Spirit is not the root of salvation but its fruit and its path (Romans 2:6–7; 8:13). Those who sow persistently to the flesh, without repentance, show they do not have the Spirit.

A direction of life. Read it in the terms Paul has already set. Eternal life is not a crop you grow; this letter has spent six chapters proving that nothing you sow can purchase it. What verse 8 describes is a direction of life. The seed a man scatters shows which field he thinks he lives in, and a person indwelt by the Spirit sows to the Spirit for the same reason a living tree puts out leaves. The harvest is not his wages. It is the full growth of a life that was given to him.

Small seeds. Which turns the verse into something usable rather than frightening. Sowing is small, repeated and unremarkable, and nobody has ever sown a field in one afternoon. This morning’s twenty minutes with the Bible open, the apology you made instead of the point you were entitled to make, the money that went quietly, the conversation you had with the difficult person at church: none of it felt like anything. That is what seed is like in the hand. The reason Christians so seldom connect their spiritual dullness to anything is that they are looking for a cause the size of the effect, and there never is one. There is a field, and there is what has been going into it for eleven years.

Is this karma? No. Karma is an impersonal law of cause and effect that no one can escape. Here a personal God is speaking, who forgives, and who laid the penalty of his people’s sin on Christ. But forgiveness does not always remove the earthly consequences of sin. David was forgiven, The LORD also has put away your sin, and yet the child died (2 Samuel 12:13–14); and the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6). Nor does every hardship mean a person is reaping a particular sin; Job and the man born blind (John 9:3) show otherwise. What this verse warns against is thinking we can sow to the flesh and escape the harvest.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sorrow in life is the harvest of personal sin (John 9:3). It means God’s moral order is real.

I sowed to the flesh for years. Is it too late? No, not if you are turning to Christ now. The harvest of eternal life does not depend on the length of your sowing but on the grace of the one who gives it: the thief on the cross sowed nothing and was with Christ in paradise that day (Luke 23:43). God can restore the years the swarming locust has eaten (Joel 2:25). Some earthly consequences may remain, and you should face them honestly, putting right what you can. But Christ has borne the eternal harvest of your sin on the cross. From today, begin to sow to the Spirit, in small seeds, and trust God with the crop.

In a sentence. Do not be deceived: God cannot be mocked. A man reaps what he sows. Whoever sows to please their flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; whoever sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.

On a Tuesday. What are you sowing today, with your time, money and attention? Sow to the Spirit. Look at the last week of your diary and bank statement and screen time, and ask which field they were planted in. Then choose one small seed to sow to the Spirit every day this week.

For worship. The one who sowed most perfectly to the Spirit reaped what we had sown. Christ planted nothing but righteousness, and was handed the harvest of our corruption on the cross. Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). He was that grain. Buried in the ground, he rose as the firstfruits of a harvest that will fill the new creation, and every believer is part of the crop. God is not mocked, and God is not stingy: he gives eternal life as a gift to those who could never have grown it.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.

And let us not grow weary of doing good. The us matters. Paul has been saying you for five chapters, and he now puts himself inside the exhortation, which means the apostle knew what it was to be tired of doing good. He does not tell them to stop being weary, either. He assumes it. The verb, enkakōmen, from enkakeō, carries the sense of losing heart, going slack, running out of the will to continue (as in 2 Corinthians 4:1). It is not a warning against wickedness but against a very ordinary exhaustion. Doing good is tiring and often unthanked. That is a mercy in itself. A Christian who is worn out from carrying burdens, restoring the fallen and giving away money is not in a state Paul finds surprising. He is in the state this verse was written for.

For in due season we will reap. The phrase is kairō idiō: at its own proper time, the season that belongs to that harvest, God’s appointed time. The harvest comes, but not always immediately. No farmer resents June for not being September. He works a field that shows him nothing for months, because the timetable was never his to set, and he knows the difference between nothing is happening and nothing is visible.

If we do not give up. The one condition, and it is not achievement. Give up is eklyō: to faint, to go limp, to collapse. A farmer who quits before harvest gets nothing. Paul does not say we shall reap if we sow enough, or well, or with the right motives. He says we shall reap if we do not stop. The whole risk in the Christian life at this point is not failure but abandonment: walking off the field in the eleventh year, three weeks before something comes up.

The people this verse belongs to. So this verse belongs to particular people, and they should be named, because they are the ones most likely to be reading it at the end of their strength. The mother who has prayed for a son for twenty-two years and has stopped expecting the phone to ring. The man who teaches eight children in a back room while the church around him talks about growth. The wife who has been gentle with a hard husband for a decade with nothing whatever to show for it. The pastor in a small town who has buried more people than he has baptised. Paul’s answer to every one of them is not encouragement about their prospects. It is a fact about the universe God made: sowing is followed by reaping, and the season is his.

So then, as we have opportunity. Then verse 10 turns the weariness outward rather than inward. Opportunity is kairon again, literally as we have time: the same word as the season in verse 9. The harvest has its season, and so does the sowing, and the sowing season is now. Life is short; opportunities pass. Which quietly disposes of the commonest evasion, since as we have opportunity does not mean when it is convenient. It means while there is still time.

Let us do good to everyone. Believers and unbelievers. Christian love is not limited to the church. Everyone forbids the church that has turned inward and does its good only where it will be appreciated by people who share its views.

And especially to those who are of the household of faith. Fellow believers, family members in God’s household, come first, just as one cares first for one’s own family. Especially forbids the sentimentality that regards a general benevolence toward mankind as an adequate substitute for helping the specific believer two streets away whose boiler has failed. It is family first, which is not the same as family only. And the word household is chosen with care, because a family does not run an application process. The claim on you is not that the person deserves it. It is that he is kin.

What it does not mean. It does not mean neglecting unbelievers. It means priorities in love.

I am exhausted. Is resting the same as giving up? No. Giving up is abandoning the field; resting is what keeps you in it. God built rest into creation, Jesus took his tired disciples away to a desolate place to rest a while (Mark 6:31), and Elijah under the broom tree was given sleep and food before he was given a task (1 Kings 19:5–8). If you are worn out, you may need to sleep, to share the work, to say no to something good, or to ask for help. None of that is unfaithfulness. What Paul warns against is losing heart: concluding that doing good is pointless and walking away. Rest, and then go back to sowing.

In a sentence. Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to all people, especially to those who belong to the family of believers.

On a Tuesday. If you are weary of doing good, tell God plainly, and ask him for fresh strength. Then do the next small good thing anyway. And look for one person in your church family who needs practical help this week, and one neighbour outside it, and do good to both.

For worship. The God who never grows weary gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength (Isaiah 40:28–29). Our Lord did good without growing weary to the end: he healed when the crowds pressed him, taught when he was hungry, washed feet on the night of his betrayal, and prayed for his enemies with his last breath. He endured the cross for the joy set before him, and the harvest of that sowing is a multitude no one can number. Our small labours are hidden in his great one, and in due season, if we do not give up, we shall reap with him, and the joy will be his and ours together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The Cross and the New Creation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
In v. 11 Paul takes the pen from his secretary and writes the closing paragraph himself, in large letters — the ancient equivalent of underlining hard enough to score the page. What he writes large is not doctrine but motive. Verse 12 says the men forcing circumcision want to make a good showing in the flesh and to avoid persecution for the cross, which had a concrete meaning in that century: Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, and circumcised converts made the whole problem disappear for everyone. Verse 13 exposes the second motive, converts as trophies, and adds the detail that collapses the programme — the men selling the law do not keep it themselves, which 5:3 said it obligates them to.

Verse 14 answers with the sharpest contrast in the letter. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows, and far be it from me is his most violent negative. The cross was not yet jewellery: it was Rome’s method for killing slaves in public, and for a Pharisee it carried the curse of Deuteronomy 21:23 that Paul quoted at 3:13. The double crucifixion he describes runs both ways — the world's offers have lost their force on him, and he has lost his standing in its eyes, which is the harder half and precisely what the Judaizers were avoiding.

Verse 15 gives the verdict: neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, but a new creation — kainē ktisis, new in kind, the age to come arriving early in a person, not a renovation of the old. Verse 16 pronounces peace and mercy on all who walk by that rule, and on the Israel of God, the most argued-over phrase in the letter. Verse 17 closes the case not with an argument but with scars — stigmata, the brand of ownership — and v. 18 ends where 1:3 began, with grace, and with the word brothers standing last in the Greek sentence before the Amen.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross as the Permanent Centre, and the Israel of God

Paul’s boast in v. 14 is the summary of everything the letter has argued. The cross is where the law’s curse was absorbed, where the old creation died and the new was born, and Reformed theology has always insisted it is not merely the entrance to the Christian life but its permanent centre — the ground the believer stands on at every moment from conversion to glory. This is Luther’s theology of the cross against a theology of glory: God’s ways are read from below, through shame and suffering, not from above through human notions of power and success.

On v. 16 everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean “and” or “even.” Read as “even the Israel of God,” the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together, are the Israel of God, which is the standard Reformed reading and is supported by 3:29 and 4:26. Read as simply “and,” a second group is in view, most naturally believing Jews. The first fits the letter’s whole argument best; the second is held by serious readers who love this book, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11. On what actually matters here nobody disagrees: whoever they are, the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation, and no one enters that number by ancestry or by a mark.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The Judaizers wanted social safety, and vv. 12–13 name it without charity: circumcising the Gentiles satisfied the synagogue and left Rome uninterested. Verse 17 answers it with the marks Paul carried from his sufferings, among them the stoning at Lystra in Galatia itself (Acts 14:19).

Now:The test v. 13 puts to a softened conviction is not whether the reason is defensible but what the adjustment costs you. And v. 17 belongs to anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something unglamorous — Paul filed his scars under the same heading as the wounds of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.

See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand. Paul takes the pen off his secretary. Letters in that world were normally dictated, with the author adding a line at the end in his own hand as a signature (2 Thessalonians 3:17); here he takes over for the whole closing paragraph, and he writes big. Possibly his eyes were poor, which would fit 4:15. Chiefly it is emphasis: the ancient equivalent of writing in bold, of underlining hard enough to score the page. What follows is the whole letter compressed, in his own handwriting, and he does not want it missed.

It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised. And what he writes large is not doctrine. It is motive. Make a good showing is euprosōpeō, literally to present a fine face, to look good outwardly, to look well in public. The false teachers cared about outward appearance and reputation.

And only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ. Then Paul names what they are actually buying with the Galatians’ circumcision: their real motive was avoiding persecution from non-Christian Jews. That is worth setting in its own century, because it turns an insult into a diagnosis. Judaism was a recognised religion under Rome, with legal protection and exemptions that other cults did not enjoy. A movement of circumcised Jews who followed a Messiah could shelter under that. A movement of uncircumcised Gentiles worshipping a crucified Jew could not, and it looked to the synagogues like apostasy and to Rome like a new and unlicensed sect. Meanwhile Jewish nationalist feeling was rising through those decades, and Jewish Christians who were seen to be dissolving the boundary paid for it at home. If Gentile converts were circumcised, Christianity looked like a Jewish sect, and the offence of the cross disappeared (5:11).

A reasonable committee. So the Judaizers were not primarily theologians. They were men under pressure, doing something explicable. Get the Gentiles circumcised and the whole problem goes away: the synagogue is satisfied, Rome is uninterested, and nobody has to be beaten. It is a solution any reasonable committee might reach.

For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law. Paul adds the detail that collapses the whole programme. He had told them in 5:3 that circumcision obligates a man to the entire code. Here he observes that the men selling it are not keeping it either. Hypocrisy: they demanded others keep the law while not keeping it themselves. So this was never a serious attempt at law-righteousness. It was a way of belonging safely, dressed in Scripture.

But they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh. Then the second motive, and it is uglier. Converts as trophies: something done to another man’s body that can be counted and reported. They wanted to count circumcisions. Every generation of ministry has its version of this: the number, the testimony repeated at conferences, the person who has become a credential.

What does the adjustment cost you? Which puts a question to anyone who has ever softened a Christian conviction and given a theological reason for it. The test is not whether your reason is defensible; the Judaizers had excellent reasons, and one of them was avoiding a beating. The test is what the adjustment costs you. Every change these men proposed made their lives easier, and the flesh has never once recommended a course of action that would get its owner persecuted. Paul’s alternative is in the next verse, and it is a cross, which is exactly what the whole manoeuvre was designed to avoid.

Is it wrong to avoid persecution if I can? Not in itself. Jesus told his disciples to flee from one town to the next when persecuted (Matthew 10:23), Paul escaped Damascus in a basket and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen, and we are to pray for peaceful lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Wisdom, tact and lawful protection are good. What is wrong is avoiding persecution by changing the message: dropping the parts of the gospel that offend, keeping quiet about Christ when silence is denial, or bending God’s commands to fit in. Ask whether you are avoiding trouble or avoiding Christ. The first may be wise; the second is the Judaizers’ path.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all Jewish Christians were insincere. Paul speaks of these particular teachers. Many Jewish believers, like Peter, James and Barnabas, shared his gospel and suffered for it.

In a sentence. See what large letters Paul uses as he writes to you with his own hand! Those who want to impress people by means of the flesh are trying to compel you to be circumcised. The only reason they do this is to avoid being persecuted for the cross of Christ. Not even those who are circumcised keep the law, yet they want you to be circumcised that they may boast about your circumcision in the flesh.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to make a good showing, at church, online, at work? Notice one place this week where you trim your faith to avoid disapproval, and ask God for courage to stop. Live for his approval, not for appearances.

For worship. The Lord Jesus never once made a good showing in the flesh. He had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2), he refused the crowd that wanted to make him king, and he walked deliberately toward the persecution every reasonable committee would have avoided. He did not save himself, so that he could save others. And he does not count his people as trophies but as children; he does not boast in our flesh but gave his own flesh for the life of the world (John 6:51). His love seeks nothing for itself and everything for us.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then took the pen himself to finish; his large letters may reflect poor eyesight or simply emphasis.

verseByVerse.quote: But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.

But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. They boast in flesh; Paul boasts in a gallows. The false teachers boasted in circumcision. Paul boasts only in the cross, the instrument of shame. And the opening phrase is mē genoito, the same violent negative he used at 2:17 and 3:21: may it never be, God forbid. He is not saying he has other grounds for boasting and modestly declines them. He is saying the thought is unthinkable. The cross is the centre of his life and message.

How strange it sounded. Feel how strange the sentence would have sounded. The cross was not yet jewellery. It was the Roman state’s instrument for killing slaves and rebels in public, deliberately obscene, so shameful that polite Roman writers avoided the word. Cicero said the very name of the cross should be far from the body of a Roman citizen, and from his thoughts, eyes and ears. And a Pharisee had the additional certainty of Deuteronomy 21:23, which Paul quoted back in 3:13: a hanged man is cursed by God. To boast in a crucifixion was, in Jewish terms, blasphemy, and in Roman terms, disgusting.

The only boast. That is the object Paul says is the only thing in the universe he will glory in. Not his conversion, which was spectacular. Not his missionary record, which was unmatched. Not his learning, his visions or his suffering. One thing, and it is something done for him rather than by him. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31).

By which the world has been crucified to me. Then he says what the cross accomplished in him personally, and it is a double death. Take the two directions separately, because they are different operations and most Christians have only had one of them done. The world here is the whole system of values, status and religion opposed to God, including religious achievement. The world has been crucified to me: through the cross it is dead to Paul, and its offers have lost their power and appeal. What it holds out, standing, security, the approval of the people whose approval you were raised to want, is not all evil, and Paul is not saying he despises it. He is saying it is dead to him. It cannot buy him any more, because he has seen the one thing it had no answer for.

And I to the world. And Paul is dead to the world: it no longer has a claim on him. He has lost his standing in its eyes too. This is the harder half, and it is the one the Judaizers were desperate to avoid. A man dead to the world is a man the world has finished assessing. He is not being ranked, because he is not a candidate. Which is precisely why he was free to write this letter and they were not. A double crucifixion. Isaac Watts’s hymn When I Survey the Wondrous Cross is built on this verse: forbid it, Lord, that I should boast, save in the death of Christ my God.

What it looks like with a mortgage. What does that look like in an ordinary life with a mortgage and a family? Not withdrawal. Paul had a trade and travelled and cared enormously about money for the poor. It looks like this: the world can still take things from you and can no longer take anything that matters from you, and it can no longer set your price. Ask what would happen if the reputation you have built quietly collapsed, not through sin, just through being overlooked or misunderstood. If the answer is that you would lose something painful but survivable, the crucifixion has been done. If the answer is that you would not know who you were, the world is still very much alive.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul hated the created world or other people. God so loved the world that he gave his only Son (John 3:16), and everything created by God is good, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). It means the world’s values no longer ruled him.

How do I boast in the cross in practice? Make it the first thing you say about yourself when you stand before God: not what you have done, but what Christ did. When you are praised, quietly give the credit to his grace. When you are accused, run to the cross rather than to your record. When you speak of your faith to others, talk about Jesus crucified and risen, not mainly about your experience or your church. Sing the hymns that look at the cross, and look at it yourself each day, slowly, until its glory crowds out the smaller glories you are tempted to chase.

In a sentence. May Paul never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to him, and he to the world.

On a Tuesday. What does the world still offer that attracts you? Look at the cross until it loses its grip. Read a passion narrative this week, slowly, and set beside it the thing you most want people to think of you.

For worship. Stand back and look at what Paul is glorying in. The Son of God, hanging on a beam outside a city, stripped, mocked, numbered with criminals, bearing a curse that belonged to other people; and there is not a throne in the history of the world that has ever been so completely a throne as that. There the love of God was shown at full strength, the justice of God was satisfied in full, the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15), and the Lamb who was slain was found worthy to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honour and glory and blessing (Revelation 5:12). The universe has one boast in it, and it is a man on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.

For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision. The verdict that ends the argument, as in 5:6. Outward religious status is irrelevant. And it is worth pairing with the two other places Paul finishes the same sentence differently. In 5:6 what counts is faith working through love; in 1 Corinthians 7:19 it is keeping the commandments of God; here, a new creation. Three answers, one thing: the question is never the mark on the body but whether God has done something.

But a new creation. What counts is being made new by God in Christ. Regeneration, not ritual. A new creation is kainē ktisis, and kainos means new in kind, not merely recent. Paul is reaching for Genesis 1, and for Isaiah’s promise of new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). What the gospel produces is not a reformed version of the old thing: not a better man, a tidied-up religion, a Judaism with the difficult parts adjusted. It is the age to come, arriving early, in a person. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). That is what made the Judaizing offer so hopeless. They were proposing an alteration to somebody who had already been raised. It is the difference between renovating a house and being born.

I do not feel like a new creation. Am I one? Being a new creation is first something God declares and does, not something you feel. The new creation has begun in you if you have been united to Christ by faith: God has given you a new heart, his Spirit lives in you, and you belong to the age to come. But the old body, the old memories, many old habits and the remaining flesh are still there, which is why it does not always feel new. Look for the marks: a new love for Christ, a new hatred of sin, new desires to please God, a new family in the church. These may be small. A newborn does not feel like a person either, but he is one, and he will grow.

And as for all who walk by this rule. Rule is kanōn: a measuring rod, a straight edge, a standard. The rule is what he has just said: not circumcision, not uncircumcision, but new creation, the rule of grace alone.

Peace and mercy be upon them. A blessing, echoing Psalm 125:5 and 128:6: peace be upon Israel. And notice the order, which is not the order of Paul’s greetings anywhere else. He normally writes grace and peace. Here mercy comes alongside peace, as though at the end of a letter this severe he wants the last word on the Galatians to be that they will be dealt with kindly.

And upon the Israel of God. This is the most argued-over phrase in the letter, and honesty is better than false confidence. Interpreters differ over whether the Israel of God means believing Jews within the church, or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. Everything turns on the small word kai, which can mean and or even. Read it as even the Israel of God, and the phrase caps the sentence: those who walk by this rule, Jew and Gentile together in Christ, are the Israel of God. Read it as simply and, and a second group is in view, most naturally Jewish believers, the believing remnant, singled out for a particular blessing at the end of a letter that has been hard on their nation’s badge.

Where Christians differ: who is the Israel of God? Some take the Israel of God to be ethnic Israel, or believing Jews, distinct from Gentile believers. Others take it as the whole church. The second reading of kai is held by serious readers who love this book and read it carefully, including many who expect a future for ethnic Israel on the strength of Romans 11 and who honour the Scriptures as fully as anyone who differs from them. Verdict: In context, Paul has spent the whole letter arguing that all believers, Jew and Gentile, are Abraham’s offspring and heirs (3:7, 29), that the Jerusalem above is our mother (4:26), and that ethnic markers count for nothing. It would be strange to end by separating believing Jews as a special group. The Israel of God is best understood as the whole people of God in Christ, the true Israel (Romans 2:28–29; Philippians 3:3). This does not cancel God’s purposes for ethnic Israel (Romans 11), but describes the church as the fulfilment of Israel.

What everyone agrees on. It is worth saying plainly that on the point that actually matters here, nobody disagrees: whoever the Israel of God is, they are those on whom peace and mercy rest, and the rule they walk by is the cross and the new creation. A man does not get into that number by ancestry or by a mark, and never has.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jews are excluded from the Israel of God. Believing Jews are at its heart.

No papers checked. And there is comfort in the phrase however it is parsed. The Galatians had been told for months that they were outsiders to the people of God, provincial latecomers who would always be second-tier. Paul’s final blessing lays peace and mercy on everyone walking by this rule, and does not check anybody’s papers on the way past.

In a sentence. Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything; what counts is the new creation. Peace and mercy to all who follow this rule, to the Israel of God.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to feel second-class among God’s people, because of your background, your past, your lack of the right experiences or credentials, remember the rule: new creation is all that counts, and peace and mercy rest on everyone who walks by it. And treat other believers the same way: do not check their papers either.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you are a new creation and part of the Israel of God. The God who said, let there be light, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). The first creation began with a word; the new creation began with a resurrection, and the risen Christ is its firstborn. One day he will say, behold, I am making all things new (Revelation 21:5), and the whole universe will match what he has already begun in his people. Until then, his peace and mercy rest on us, not because of any mark in our flesh, but because of the marks in his.
verseByVerse.note: Interpreters differ over whether “the Israel of God” means believing Jews or the whole church, Jew and Gentile together. The more persuasive reading is the whole church (compare 3:29).

verseByVerse.quote: From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

From now on let no one cause me trouble. It sounds abrupt, almost weary. Paul has said all he needs to; let the controversy end. There is a quiet finality in from now on. The case is closed. He has argued covenants, chronology, Abraham, Hagar and the Spirit for six chapters, and at the end he simply shows the scars.

For I bear on my body the marks of Jesus. The reason is in the word he chooses. The marks are stigmata, and in that world a stigma was a brand: burned or cut into the skin of a slave to show whose he was, into a soldier to show whose army, into a temple servant to show whose god. Paul’s were the scars left by beatings and stoning. Now put that against the argument of the whole letter. The Judaizers wanted a mark cut into Gentile flesh to prove ownership and belonging. Paul says: I have marks. I did not choose them, and they were put there by people trying to stop me. The rods at Philippi (Acts 16:22). The stones at Lystra, in Galatia itself, where some of those hearing this letter may have watched him dragged out of their own town and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Those are his credentials, and they settle the question of whose he is far more conclusively than circumcision ever could. The false teachers wanted the mark of circumcision; Paul bears the marks of suffering for Christ, showing whose slave he is.

Marks that are honoured. That is worth pausing on for anyone whose faithfulness has cost them something visible and unglamorous: a career that went nowhere because of a conviction, a family that cooled, a body worn out in a small work nobody counted. Those marks are not evidence of a failure to manage life well. Paul called his the marks of Jesus, and expected them to be honoured.

Where Christians differ: the stigmata. Some medieval saints, such as Francis of Assisi, were said to receive the stigmata: wounds like Christ’s, miraculously appearing on their hands and feet, seen as a sign of special holiness. Verdict: Paul’s marks were the ordinary scars of persecution suffered for preaching Christ, not miraculous wounds. Scripture nowhere teaches miraculous stigmata or treats them as a sign of holiness. The true marks of belonging to Christ are faith, love, holiness and willingness to suffer for him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns favour with God. It means faithful suffering shows whose we are.

I have never suffered for Christ like this. Am I a lesser Christian? No. Your standing with God rests on Christ’s wounds, not yours, and God assigns different paths to different servants. Many Christians in quiet places live long lives without beatings or prison, and they are not second-class. But every believer bears some marks: the cost of honesty at work, the friend lost over your faith, the self-denial nobody sees, the patience in a hard marriage, the ridicule for your convictions. Do not despise those small marks, and do not go looking for dramatic ones. Be faithful where you are, pray for those who suffer more (Hebrews 13:3), and be ready if the cost rises.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen. And look at what the last word is. Not foolish Galatians, which is how the argument started; not a final warning; not the name of an opponent. After all the sharp words, he calls them brothers. In the Greek the sentence ends, just before the Amen, with brothers. The man who wrote an anathema in the first chapter signs off calling them family.

Grace at both ends. The letter that began with grace (1:3, 6) ends with grace, and everything between the two is an argument that nothing may be added to it. Not circumcision, not a calendar, not the endorsement of Jerusalem, not the record of the man reading this. The letter closes exactly where it opened, because there is nowhere else for a Christian to stand.

In a sentence. From now on, let no one cause Paul trouble, for he bears on his body the marks of Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers and sisters. Amen.

On a Tuesday. Are you willing to bear marks for Jesus: misunderstanding, loss, opposition? Then end the day resting in his grace. Before you sleep tonight, say the last verse of Galatians over yourself and over the people you love.

For worship. So the last thing Galatians does is hold up its subject one more time. A Son sent in the fullness of time, born of a woman and under the law; who kept every clause of it and then went out to a tree and was made a curse, so that the blessing sworn to Abraham could reach a farmer in Lystra with no ancestry and no merit and nothing to bring; who bought slaves out of the market, cancelled the debt, gave them his own name, put his Spirit in their hearts and taught them to say Father. He bears marks too: in his hands, his feet and his side, and he will bear them for ever, the only man-made things in heaven. Nothing was cheapened to do it. Everything was paid. And the whole of it, from first to last, was grace, which is why the letter can end with the word it began with, and there is nothing left to add. Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The “marks” were the scars left by beatings and stoning — like the brands on a slave showing whom he belonged to.

6.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, if anyone is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness. Keep watch on yourself, lest you too be tempted.<sup>2</sup>Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.<sup>3</sup>For if anyone thinks he is something, when he is nothing, he deceives himself.<sup>4</sup>But let each one test his own work, and then his reason to boast will be in himself alone and not in his neighbor.<sup>5</sup>For each will have to bear his own load.<sup>6</sup>Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches.<sup>7</sup>Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.<sup>8</sup>For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.<sup>9</sup>And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.<sup>10</sup>So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith.<sup>11</sup>See with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand.<sup>12</sup>It is those who want to make a good showing in the flesh who would force you to be circumcised, and only in order that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.<sup>13</sup>For even those who are circumcised do not themselves keep the law, but they desire to have you circumcised that they may boast in your flesh.<sup>14</sup>But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.<sup>15</sup>For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.<sup>16</sup>And as for all who walk by this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God.<sup>17</sup>From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.<sup>18</sup>The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.
